sens: The motive, the reason why something happens or must be said
The manner, the mode or the way in which something is accomplished
The subject, what is being talked about or what is in question
H1700.detail:
1. The motive or reason for acting: when Job says he will "present his cause" to God (Job 5:8), he means that he will present to God the reasons for his distress, the motive for his complaint. It is the cause in the sense of what justifies an action or a word.
2. The manner or way of doing: when it is said that Christ is a "priest in the order of Melchizedek" (Psalms 110:4), it designates the way, the particular mode by which he exercises his priesthood. This meaning is close to the first but emphasizes the "how" rather than the "why."
3. The subject or theme being discussed: in Ecclesiastes 3:18, the author says "concerning the sons of man," meaning he is stating something that concerns humanity. It is the cause as the matter being treated, what is being discoursed upon.
H1700.origine: The Hebrew word דִּבְרָה (dibrah) comes from the root דברדברdabbar, "to speak" (from which the name דָּבָר, dabar, "word, thing" is derived). A cause or motive is primarily what is stated or what is the reason for it: one "speaks" a cause, one "presents" it. The meaning has extended from the word itself to the reason for speaking, then to any motive or subject.
H1700.emploi: This word appears five times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in the wisdom literature (Job, Psalms, Ecclesiastes). It carries closely related but distinct nuances: sometimes "cause" in the sense of motive or reason (Job 5:8: present his cause), sometimes "manner" or "mode" (Psalms 110:4: in the manner of), sometimes "subject" or "theme" (Ecclesiastes 3:18: concerning). The context of wisdom literature shows that the word is used to express the reasons for things, the way God orders the world, and the subjects for reflection for the wise man.
H1700.portee: This word invites the reader to understand that faith also consists of presenting to God the true reasons for our concerns (as Job does), and seeking the "why" of the trials He allows. It reminds us that everything that happens has a cause in God's plan, even when we do not initially see it (Ecclesiastes 7:14).

sens: Reason or motive for an action, an event
Intention or goal pursued
End aimed at, that for which one acts
H1701.detail:
1. The word designates the deep reason for why something happens or is done. In Daniel 2:30, the secret has been revealed, and the cause is that "the explanation may be given to the king": this is the motive for the revelation.
2. It also expresses the intention or goal that one seeks to achieve. In Daniel 4:17, the divine decree is given "so that the living may know that the Most High rules": the cause is this knowledge that is intended to be produced in men.
3. More broadly, it is the end aimed at, that towards which an action or word tends. The word emphasizes the deep "why": not just what happens, but for what reason or purpose.
H1701.origine: This Aramaic word comes from the same root as the corresponding Hebrew word (H1700) and literally means "word" or "matter." Like in Hebrew, it has taken on the meaning of "reason" or "motive": the word that explains why one acts, the discourse that justifies. This root is found in several Semitic words designating speech or the matter at hand.
H1701.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Bible, both times in Aramaic in the book of Daniel (2:30 and 4:17). In these two uses, it introduces the divine purpose or motive: why God reveals a secret to Daniel, why He issues a decree to kings. The context is always that of the fulfillment of divine will and understanding the hidden reasons behind events. The word carries a theological significance: it helps the reader grasp that everything that happens has a deep reason intended by God.
H1701.portee: This word reminds us that no event is without cause or purpose in God's design. For the reader of Daniel, it invites one to seek not only what happens but why it happens, what divine intention lies behind it. It is an invitation to faith: to recognize that behind decrees and revelations lies a wise and loving motive from the Most High.

sens: Floating structure made of wood or materials tied together to transport goods on water
Means of maritime transport of logs or cargo
H1702.detail:
1. A raft is a floating platform constructed by tying together beams or logs of wood, intended to float on water and carry a load. In 1 Kings 5:9, King Solomon receives wood from Lebanon that his servants "will bring down from Lebanon to the sea, and I will send it by sea on rafts": the cedar logs, too heavy to be transported otherwise, are thus assembled into rafts and entrusted to the sea to reach their destination.
2. The raft embodies the idea of efficient and organized maritime transport: rather than loading traditional ships, a floating structure is created suited to the type of cargo being transported, particularly construction materials like wood.
H1702.origine: The Hebrew word דֹּבְרוֹת (dobevrah) comes from the root דָּבַר which evokes the action of binding or assembling together, hence the natural image of elements joined to form a floating structure. It is a concrete word, rooted in the realities of maritime trade in the ancient Levant, where the transport of wood from Lebanon by sea was an established and strategic practice.
H1702.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in 1 Kings 5:9. It is set in the context of the market between King Solomon and Hiram of Tyre: Hiram provides the wood and labor for the construction of the Temple in Jerusalem, and in return, Solomon commits to supplying Tyre's court. The rafts are the logistical vector of this international trade, reflecting the sophisticated organization of Levantine commerce in the 10th century BCE.
H1702.portee: This passage reveals that God provides for the construction of His Temple through concrete and human means: the alliance between Solomon and Hiram, facilitated by maritime transport, shows how God works through commercial relationships and cooperation between peoples. It is a reminder that faith does not oppose practical organization and the intelligent use of natural resources.

sens: A statement pronounced by someone
A command or divine instruction
A transmitted message
A promise or solemn declaration
H1703.detail:
1. The word designates a spoken word, a statement — what comes out of someone's mouth. In Deuteronomy 33:3, Moses refers to the "words" that the people received from the hand of God: these are the divine words that were transmitted to them, the teachings and instructions of the Lord.
2. The term is often used for the words of God, His commandments, His instructions — the word as that which orders, guides, shapes the life of the chosen people.
3. It is also a message carrying meaning, that which communicates a thought, a will, a direction.
4. A word can be a promise or a solemn declaration, something that one holds, that one keeps in the heart.
H1703.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the action of speaking, of pronouncing words. In biblical Hebrew, the word is never a mere sound emission: it is creation, it accomplishes what it states, it has its own force. That is why the "word of God" is often at the heart of biblical theology — it creates, it judges, it saves.
H1703.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Deuteronomy 33:3, where it refers to the words of God received by the people of Israel. In this context of Moses' final speech before his death, the "words" refer to the entirety of the Law, the divine instructions that God's chosen people had the privilege to receive. It is a word that distinguishes Israel, binding it to its God.
H1703.portee: Understanding that the words of God are not mere information, but a word that acts, that creates, that directs life. It is a call to listen and keep this word in the heart, to recognize it as a precious gift from the Lord within His people.

sens: Man of the tribe of Dan, father of Shelomith
H1704.detail: Dibri is a Danite of whom we know only one thing: he is the father of Shelomith, the mother of the young man who blasphemed the name of God in the wilderness. His name appears only once in the entire Bible, in Leviticus 24:11, during the account of this serious incident. Although discreet, this name marks an important moment in Israel's history in the wilderness, the moment when God precisely established the law against blasphemy.
H1704.origine: The name Dibri literally means "my word" in Hebrew, formed from the root דברdabar (word, thing). It is a theophoric name, where the possessive "my" refers to God: it carries the idea of a word from God or a divine matter. In the biblical context, this type of name expresses the father's relationship to God at the time of the child's birth.
H1704.emploi: Dibri appears only once in the Bible, in Leviticus 24:11. He is mentioned solely as the father of Shelomith, in the account where her son commits blasphemy against the divine name. This passage establishes the first written law against blasphemy and the death penalty it incurs. Although Dibri himself does not speak or act in the text, his presence in this genealogy allows the incident to be situated within the tribe of Dan and reminds us that even Israelite families could produce serious transgressors.
H1704.portee: This name reminds the reader that no one, regardless of their genealogy or belonging to Israel, is spared from the temptation of serious sin. The blasphemy of Shelomith's son shows that the boundary between the people of God and major transgression can be crossed from within. It is a warning to every generation: the name of the Lord must be treated with deep reverence and absolute respect.

sens: City in Galilee assigned to the Levites
H1705.detail: Dabrath is a city located at the western foot of Mount Tabor, in the territory of Issachar. It is listed among the cities that God granted to the Levites for them to dwell in, along with their surrounding pastures. The name means "word" in Hebrew, but it refers here to a specific geographical location in ancient Galilee.
H1705.origine: The Hebrew name Dabrath comes from the root דבר (dabar), which means "word" or "thing said." It is an ancient place name, perhaps given in reference to an event or a sanctuary where the word of God was proclaimed.
H1705.emploi: Dabrath appears three times in the Bible: twice in the account of the territorial distribution of the Promised Land (Joshua 19:12 and 21:28) and once in the parallel account in Chronicles (1 Chronicles 6:72). It is mentioned as one of the Levitical cities assigned to the tribe of Issachar. This allocation showed how the Levites, without their own territorial inheritance, received habitable cities among the lands of other tribes.

sens: sweet and golden substance produced by bees
appreciated food, often offered as a gift
symbol of the richness and prosperity of the promised land
sweetness to the taste, source of pleasure
sweet and pleasant word or teaching
image of excellence and divine grace
H1706.detail:
1. Honey is the nectar produced by bees from which a sweet food is derived: Samson finds it in the carcass of a lion (Judges 14:8-9), and Jonathan tastes a bit, which restores his strength and clarity (1 Samuel 14:29).
2. It is a product of great value, offered as a gift to an important person, as when Israel sends honey among the best fruits of the land to the governor of Egypt (Genesis 43:11).
3. Honey symbolizes the abundance and fertility of the promised land: God promises Israel a land "flowing with milk and honey" (Numbers 14:8, Deuteronomy 31:20), an image of the blessing and wealth that God offers to His people.
4. Its sweet taste makes it extremely pleasant: the psalmist says that God's words are "sweeter to my mouth than honey" (Psalms 119:103), comparing the excellence of the divine word to the pleasure of honey.
5. The sweetness of honey becomes an image for wise words and teachings that comfort: "Pleasant words are a honeycomb, sweet to the soul" (Proverbs 16:24), showing how good words nourish the spirit as honey nourishes the body.
6. Finally, honey symbolizes grace and divine blessings: Ezekiel reports that God gave honey to Israel among precious goods (Ezekiel 16:13), an image of the generosity and sweetness of God's favor towards His people.
H1706.origine: The Hebrew word דְּבַשׁ (devash) comes from an ancient root designating the liquid and sweet substance produced by bees. In biblical Hebrew, honey is one of the luxury and wealth foods, a valued product in ancient Near Eastern culture. The biblical context shows that honey was known in Palestine and was used both for food and for preserving food or for religious purposes.
H1706.emploi: The word honey appears 54 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in historical, poetic, and prophetic books. It primarily designates the concrete product produced by bees: Samson discovers it in a lion's carcass (Judges 14:8-9), and Jonathan encounters it in a field. But very quickly, honey becomes an image of wealth and blessing: the expression "land flowing with milk and honey" (Exodus 3:8, Numbers 14:8, Deuteronomy 31:20) describes God's divine promise of a fertile and generous land. In Psalms and Proverbs, honey symbolizes the sweetness of the divine word and wisdom: "Your words are sweeter than honey" (Psalms 119:103), "Pleasant words are sweet honey" (Proverbs 16:24). Ezekiel uses it to evoke the material blessings that God granted to Israel (Ezekiel 16:13-19). The word remains always concrete and tangible: it is a food that one tastes, that one offers, whose sweetness one savors, but which constantly refers to God's love and generosity.
H1706.portee: Honey reminds the believer that God's promises are not abstract: they offer a good, rich, and flavorful life, a land that produces abundance. The word of God itself is described as sweeter than honey, inviting the reader to desire to know God and His commandments with the same intensity as one desires to taste delicious food. It is an invitation to associate obedience to faith with something beautiful and sweet, not with austerity or deprivation.

sens: Fleshy and fatty protuberance on the back of the camel
That which protrudes, that which juts out
H1707.detail: 1. The hump is the protuberance of the camel — this mass of flesh and fat that rises on its back and allows it to store energy to cross deserts. In Isaiah 30:6, it is on these humps that caravans load their treasures to transport them across Arabia. The camel with its hump becomes the image of a beast capable of carrying heavy loads over long distances. 2. Figuratively, the word can refer to any protrusion, any visible bulge — that which makes a surface swell or bulge. It is a concrete image, drawn from the observation of desert animals that the Israelites encountered.
H1707.origine: The Hebrew word דַּבֶּשֶׁת comes from a root that evokes that which rises or protrudes. In Hebrew, the names of animals and their distinctive characteristics are often formed directly from a descriptive root. The camel's hump was well known in the ancient Near East, as the camel was the major transport animal on caravan routes and in the desert regions of the Levant and Arabia.
H1707.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 30:6. The context is that of a prophetic vision where Isaiah describes the perils of traveling in a foreign land — here probably towards Egypt. The caravans carry their treasures on the humps of the camels, which shows the load that this animal can bear and underscores the importance of the goods transported. The word is thus used in a concrete context of ancient Near Eastern commercial geography.
H1707.portee: This small word reminds us of the wisdom of the created world: God has given the camel physical characteristics suited to the hostile environment of the desert. For the reader, the hump is not an insignificant detail in Isaiah's picture — it embodies divine providence that equips creatures with the means to survive and serve humanity. It is also an image of faithfulness to the divine plan, even in the midst of uncertainty and travel.

sens: City of the tribe of Zebulun in Canaan
H1708.detail: Dabbéscheth is a border locality of the tribe of Zebulun in the land of Canaan. It is mentioned only once in the Bible, during the division of the lands among the tribes of Israel: it is located on the southern boundary of Zebulun's territory, between Sarid to the east and the brook of Jokneam to the west (Joshua 19:11).
H1708.origine: The name Dabbéscheth literally means "hill" or "place of a hill," evoking a mountainous relief. It is a geographical toponym designating a city or a locality rather than a person.
H1708.emploi: Dabbéscheth appears only once in the biblical text, in Joshua 19:11, during the description of the territorial boundaries of the tribe of Zebulun. It is identified as a geographical landmark on the southern boundary of the territory assigned to this tribe during the conquest and division of Canaan under Joshua.

sens: Aquatic animal, creature of the waters
Gate of Jerusalem through which one accessed the fish market
H1709G.detail:
1. The fish is an animal that lives in water. It is one of the creatures of God's creation. In the Bible, fish also served as food for the people of Israel, and they were sold in the markets of the great cities.
2. The Fish Gate is a famous gate of Jerusalem, named because it provided access to the city's fish market. It was located in the walls of Jerusalem and was an important entrance. Nehemiah speaks of its reconstruction (Nehemiah 3:3), and it is also mentioned during the consecration of the walls (Nehemiah 12:39). Zephaniah prophesies lamentations at this gate on the day of judgment (Zephaniah 1:10).
H1709G.origine: The Hebrew word dag comes from a root that simply designates that which swims and lives in water. It is an ancient and common word in Hebrew for fish. It has no other specific use in the Bible, except for the designation of this famous gate of Jerusalem.
H1709G.emploi: The word "fish" appears 4 times in the provided usages, and in each case, it refers to the Fish Gate, one of the gates of Jerusalem. This gate is named because it led to the market where fish were sold. It is seen rebuilt under Nehemiah after the exile (Nehemiah 3:3), it is mentioned during the consecration of the rebuilt walls (Nehemiah 12:39), and the prophet Zephaniah announces lamentations there on the day of divine judgment (Zephaniah 1:10). It was also a fortified place since the time of King Hezekiah (2 Chronicles 33:14).

sens: Aquatic animal living in fresh or salt waters
Living creature under the power and dominion of man
Food consumed by peoples
Symbol of fragility before divine judgments
H1709H.detail:
1. The fish is simply an animal that lives in water, in seas and rivers. It is a living creature among many others in the animal world.
2. In God's design, fish are placed under man's control: after the flood, God tells Noah that the fish of the sea, like all animals, are "delivered into your hands" (Genesis 9:2). They are part of the creatures subject to human authority.
3. Fish are food that peoples consume and exchange. The Israelites remembered the fish of Egypt that they ate freely (Numbers 11:22), and in Jerusalem, merchants sold fish (Nehemiah 13:16).
4. The fish can also symbolize vulnerability in the face of disasters: when God's judgments unfold, the fish of the sea tremble and die just like man (Ezekiel 38:20; Hosea 4:3). The great fish that swallows Jonah (Jonah 2:1) becomes the instrument of divine judgment and grace.
H1709H.origine: The word "dag" in Hebrew simply designates the fish. It comes from a root that, in Semitic languages, refers to aquatic life. The word is common throughout biblical Hebrew to designate any animal living in water, regardless of size or species. Its concrete and everyday usage reflects the importance of fish in the diet and life of the peoples of the ancient Near East.
H1709H.emploi: The word "fish" appears 14 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, in various contexts that reveal its importance. It first appears in inventories of creation where fish are listed alongside other creatures (Psalms 8:9; 1 Kings 4:33): it is an element of the created world that God made and maintains order over. Fish also appear in texts that speak of human dominion over creatures (Genesis 9:2), reminding us that even aquatic animals are subject to man. As food, it appears in connection with daily life and abundance (Numbers 11:22; Nehemiah 13:16). Finally, in the prophets, fish become a symbol of fragility during eschatological disasters: in the judgments declared by Ezekiel, Hosea, and Zephaniah, fish die or tremble along with men and all of creation, underscoring the universality of divine judgments.
H1709H.portee: The fish reminds us that man has received from God authority over all creatures, a responsibility and privilege at the same time. But its mention in prophetic judgment texts warns that all creation shares the consequences of sin and human actions: nothing remains indifferent in the eyes of God. The fish, a silent and submissive creature, invites the reader to recognize their own dependence on the Creator and to take the prophetic word seriously.

sens: Aquatic animal with scales and fins, living creature of the seas and rivers
Food consumed by people near the water
Creature subject to man's authority according to divine design
Victim of God's plagues or judgments
H1710.detail:
1. The fish is primarily the aquatic animal as it exists in nature — a living creature of the waters, equipped with scales and capable of swimming. The Bible mentions it among the creatures that God made and recognizes as His own (Psalms 105:29).

2. The fish is also an important food source. The Egyptians regularly eat it for free, to the point that the Israelites, in the desert, nostalgically remember the fish of Egypt that they devoured without effort (Numbers 11:5).

3. From a religious and theological perspective, the fish enters into the created order where God gives man authority: God says that man must rule "over the fish of the sea" (Genesis 1:26). This is part of the human responsibility inscribed in creation.

4. In the context of judgment, the fish becomes an indicator of the plagues: when God strikes Egypt, the fish of the Nile perish, showing how the punishment reaches all of creation (Exodus 7:18). Similarly, when a restorative judgment comes, there is "a great quantity of fish" (Ezekiel 47:9).
H1710.origine: The word הָדָגָה (dagah) is a feminine Hebrew noun that simply means "fish." It comes from a root that denotes the act of fishing or multiplying in water. The word belongs to the everyday vocabulary of creation and daily life in the land of Israel. It does not derive from a metaphorical image but directly names the well-known aquatic creature of the biblical peoples living near the Mediterranean and the Nile.
H1710.emploi: The word appears 13 times in the Old Testament, mainly in historical and prophetic books. It first appears in the creation narrative (Genesis 1:26-28), where God places the fish under human authority. Exodus and Numbers use it in the context of daily life (food, plagues of Egypt). Ezekiel employs it very symbolically: the fish of the Nile attached to Pharaoh's scales become an image of judgment against Egypt (Ezekiel 29:4), while the multiplication of fish marks the return of blessing and life (Ezekiel 47:9-10). Jonah mentions the fish of the deep (Jonah 2:2). The word thus retains its concrete reality while serving as a theological instrument to express judgment or restoration.
H1710.portee: For the believer, the fish reminds us that every living creature is God's creation and remains under His sovereign gaze. In creation, it is a sign of the authority entrusted to man — an authority that must be exercised with responsibility, not arbitrarily. In the plagues of Egypt, the dead fish teach that God's judgment extends to all creation when sin demands His intervention. And in Ezekiel's prophetic vision, the proliferating fish is a promise that God restores life and fertility in a restored world.

sens: to grow in number, to increase in quantity
to prosper, to grow abundantly
H1711.detail:
1. To multiply literally means that something increases in number or quantity — here, the children of Joseph grow in number and fill the land. This is the basic meaning of the verb: to go from few to many. In Genesis 48:16, Jacob blesses his grandsons by asking that they "multiply abundantly in the midst of the land" — an image of fertility and demographic growth, like a divine blessing that causes a family to prosper.
2. The verb also carries the idea of prosperity and flourishing: to multiply is not just to count more, but to grow with abundance and strength. Jacob's blessing expresses a desire that his descendants not only be born in great numbers but that they establish themselves solidly and flourish in the promised land.
H1711.origine: The verb comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of growth and increase. The word belongs to the family of terms related to fertility and multiplication — a central theme in the biblical promise: God promises Abraham a numerous offspring (Genesis 13:16; 22:17). This blessing of multiplication is a signature of the divine covenant, marking the transition from few to many, from barren to fertile.
H1711.emploi: This verb appears only once in Genesis 48:16, in the patriarchal blessing that Jacob pronounces over Ephraim and Manasseh, the sons of Joseph. Jacob asks the angel who has protected him all his life to bless these children so that they may multiply abundantly. This context shows that the verb is used in the solemn framework of a divine blessing, evoking the promise made to Abraham to give him an innumerable offspring. Multiplication here is an expression of God's faithfulness to His word.
H1711.portee: This verb reminds us that divine blessing manifests itself through growth and prosperity — not only of material goods but especially of family and descendants. For the believer, to multiply speaks of God's work that makes fruitful and establishes His people. It is an invitation to trust that God fulfills His promises and that His blessing produces real and lasting growth.

sens: Pagan deity worshiped by the Philistines
God represented with a body that is half-human, half-fish
God of fertility and harvests
H1712.detail:
1. Dagon is a central deity of Philistine worship, revered as their main god. The Philistines offered him significant sacrifices and attributed their military victories to him, as when they credited Dagon with delivering Samson into their hands (Judges 16:23).
2. According to ancient tradition, Dagon was represented as a hybrid creature, half-human and half-aquatic, with the face and hands of a man and the tail of a fish. This representation reflects his connection to water and fertility.
3. Dagon is worshiped as a god of fertility and harvests, which explains his importance among the Philistines, a people established in a coastal and agricultural region. His worship was inseparable from the hope of abundance and prosperity.
H1712.origine: The name Dagon literally means "fish" in Hebrew. This god originated from ancient Mesopotamia and the Syro-Palestinian world, where he was worshiped long before the Philistines settled in Canaan. The Philistines adopted this worship and made it one of the major deities of their pantheon. The link with the fish reflects the economic and religious importance of fishing and fertility in coastal regions.
H1712.emploi: Dagon appears in the Bible primarily in two historical contexts: first during the time of Samson (Judges 16:23), where the Philistines celebrate his feast thinking he has delivered them from their enemy; then during the captivity of the Ark of the Covenant (1 Samuel 5:2-7), where his temple in Ashdod becomes the site of supernatural events. The statue of Dagon falls face down before the Ark, then breaks in two, with its head and hands detached. These accounts illustrate the confrontation between the God of Israel and the deities of the pagan nations, demonstrating the superiority of the true God.
H1712.portee: These passages reveal that the idols worshiped by surrounding peoples are merely representations without real power. The humiliation of Dagon before the Ark of the Lord teaches the reader that only the God of Israel is truly powerful and worthy of worship. It is a call to reject false deities and to recognize the absolute authority of the living God over all things.

sens: To appear brightly, to be particularly noticeable among others
To have an appearance or look that catches the eye
To be conspicuous, to stand out from the crowd
H1713A.detail:
1. The verb דָּגַל primarily evokes the idea of showing oneself, becoming visible or remarkable. In Song of Solomon 5:10, the beloved speaks of her beloved who "stands out among ten thousand": this image portrays someone whose beauty, presence, or demeanor makes them stand out from all others, like a banner flying above a crowd.

2. The word also carries the idea of shining or having a particular brilliance. It can be compared to the root degel (banner), which reinforces this notion of striking visibility, something that demands attention.

3. In a broader sense, it conveys the idea of excellence or distinction: not only is the person seen, but they are seen as superior or particularly attractive in the eyes of the observer.
H1713A.origine: The root דָּגַל is likely related to דֶּגֶל (degel), which means "banner" or "flag" in Hebrew. This connection of imagery is revealing: a banner is something that stands tall, is visible from afar, and attracts attention. The verb דָּגַל thus borrows from this image the idea of striking visibility and remarkable distinction.
H1713A.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Old Testament, in Song of Solomon 5:10. It is the heartfelt cry of the bride describing the one she loves: white and ruddy, he stands out among ten thousand. The rarity of the word makes it a particularly chosen term, used in a poetic and romantic context to express that the beloved is not only visible but remarkable among all, as if he shines with his own light.
H1713A.portee: For the reader, this word invites meditation on what truly makes a person or a life remarkable. Is it not less the outward appearance than the inner beauty — faithfulness, kindness, the righteousness of the heart — that truly makes one "stand out"? In an age where everyone seeks to "be noticed," this term reminds us that true distinction comes from who we are deeply.

sens: To plant, lift a banner or standard (military or rallying symbol)
To adorn with banners, to have banners
To serve as a sign of victory or gathering
H1713B.detail:
1. The most concrete meaning is that of a military action: raising a flag, a standard on the battlefield to rally the troops, mark a position, or signify a victory. It is a gesture of power and affirmation. In Psalms 20:6, the psalmist says, "We will lift the standard in the name of our God": he evokes that moment when the people gather under the sign of the Lord's presence and victory.
2. By extension, the verb describes the action of adorning, embellishing with banners, or simply being accompanied by banners. In Song of Solomon 6:4 and 6:10, the beloved is said to be "terrible as an army with banners": the image is that of an army deployed in battle order, impressive in its organization and collective strength.
H1713B.origine: The verb comes from the root דגל (dgl) and is related to the noun דגל (dagal), which specifically denotes a banner or standard. This root evokes the idea of something that is seen, that shines, that stands high to be visible from afar. The word is rooted in the military and civil life of the ancient Near East, where banners were essential markers of territory, identity, and rallying.
H1713B.emploi: The verb appears three times in the Hebrew Bible, all in situations of celebration or admiration. In Psalms 20:6, it is a promise of victory: we will lift the standard in the name of God after His salvation, manifesting joy and confidence. In the two verses from Song of Solomon (6:4 and 6:10), the term takes on a poetic hue: it evokes the power and brilliance of the beloved, compared to an army arranged in battle order under its banners. The biblical usage thus unites the concrete military idea with images of strength, beauty, and spiritual victory.
H1713B.portee: This word reminds the believer that victory and gathering come through visible signs: standards, symbols that embody our faithfulness and hope. Raising the standard of God is to publicly proclaim that we align ourselves under His name and promise. It also recognizes that faith has a collective dimension, that we do not walk alone but in the procession of those who identify with the same rallying sign.

sens: Standard or flag that a group carries to recognize and gather together
Mark of identity of a tribe or military division
H1714.detail:
1. A banner is a flag or standard that a group carries and raises to see and recognize themselves from afar. In the desert, during the journey from Egypt to Canaan, each tribe of Israel had its own banner: "each by its own camp, each near its own banner, according to their divisions" (Numbers 1:52). It was the signal for knowing where to go, where to regroup, where to follow others.
2. The banner also served to identify a tribe and mark its rank in the order of march. When the Israelites moved through the desert, "they obeyed all the commands of the Lord... Thus they camped, according to their banners; and thus they set out, each according to their family" (Numbers 2:34). Each banner was the rallying point and the symbol of unity.
H1714.origine: The Hebrew word דֶּגֶל (degel) comes from a root that evokes the idea of "lifting," "showing," "distinguishing." A banner is primarily something that is raised and shown: it is brandished so that it can be seen. It is a visible sign, a marker of identity and order. The word is used mainly in military and organizational contexts.
H1714.emploi: The word appears 14 times in the Bible, almost always in the book of Numbers, in chapters 1, 2, and 10. It describes the organization of the twelve tribes of Israel in the desert: each has its banner (Numbers 2:2, 2:3, 2:10, 2:25, 2:31), and the Levites also (Numbers 2:17). The banners regulate the order of the camp and the order of march: "The banner of the camp of Reuben set out, with its divisions" (Numbers 10:18). One occurrence stands out from this context: Song of Solomon 2:4, where "His banner over me is love," used figuratively to signify being covered or marked by someone's love.
H1714.portee: For the believer, the banner reminds us that God has organized His people with order and clarity. Everyone knows where they are, to whom they belong, and where to go. It also symbolizes belonging and protection: under the banner of a tribe, one is recognized, one is not lost. In the figurative sense (Song of Solomon 2:4), it becomes the image of what marks and covers us — the love of God that makes us His own.

sens: Cereal grain, particularly wheat, cultivated and harvested for food
Wheat harvest, crop
Subsistence, staple food
Wealth and divine blessing
Gift or confiscated property
H1715.detail:
1. Wheat refers to the cereal grain that Israel cultivates and harvests. It is the wheat that is ground into flour to make bread, an essential food. In Genesis 27:28, the father blesses his son by wishing him "abundant wheat and wine," showing that wheat is a concrete and material blessing.

2. Wheat can also refer to the entire harvest, the product of the fields at the time of harvest. Joel speaks of wheat that "rejoices" in the fields (Joel 1:10-17), evoking the plants that have grown and are ready to be harvested.

3. Wheat represents daily sustenance, the necessary food for living. When Hosea announces that God will take back "His wheat in its time" (Hosea 2:11), he threatens to remove vital necessities: this is a form of punishment through famine.

4. Wheat embodies the wealth and blessing that God grants to His people. In Deuteronomy 11:14, God promises to give wheat as a sign of His favor; conversely, the loss of wheat signals divine curse.

5. Wheat can be a mandatory offering or confiscated property. The tithes of wheat (Deuteronomy 12:17) are due to God; when Hosea 2:11 says that God will take back His wheat, it evokes a previously granted good, now taken away to punish unfaithfulness.
H1715.origine: The Hebrew word דָּגָן comes from the root דְגַן meaning "to nourish, sustain." Wheat is literally what nourishes. The word is specifically related to agriculture in the Levant: it is the cultivated grain, distinct from the bread or flour that results from it. In ancient translations of the Old Testament into Greek (the Septuagint), this Hebrew word is often rendered by σῖτος (sîtos), which has the same meaning. The family of דָּגָן encompasses the idea of food and sustenance.
H1715.emploi: The word appears about forty times in the Old Testament, mainly in the books of law (Deuteronomy), history (Chronicles, Nehemiah), and prophecy (Hosea, Joel, Ezekiel). It regularly occurs in the context of tithes and offerings due to God: wheat, along with new wine and oil, forms the trio of staple products that Israel must dedicate (Deuteronomy 12:17; Nehemiah 10:39). Wheat also appears in blessings (Genesis 27:28; Deuteronomy 33:28) and curses (Hosea 2:11; Joel 1:10), reflecting the link between the wheat harvest and God's favor or anger. In the lamentations, the absence of wheat symbolizes desolation (Lamentations 2:12).
H1715.portee: Wheat reminds us that our material needs — bread, daily food — come from the hand of God and not from our own strength. It is a symbol of covenant: in Israel, the first fruits of wheat are a recognition that everything comes from God. When the Bible threatens to take back the wheat, it teaches us that material blessing depends on our faithfulness to God. Wheat invites us to see our daily bread as a gift from God, not a personal acquisition.

sens: To cover eggs to hatch them
To gather and protect one's young
To accumulate something secretly (by extension)
H1716.detail:
1. To cover is what a mother bird does when she sits on her eggs to keep them warm and hatch them. It is the concrete, instinctive action of the animal that protects its offspring. Isaiah 34:15 speaks of the serpent that "covers" its eggs in the shade, an image of nature continuing its course.
2. To cover also means to gather and keep one's young close. The word evokes this protective closeness and the maternal or paternal instinct. The bird covers to nourish and defend its brood.
3. In a figurative sense, the word describes the accumulation of something in secret, as if one were "covering" it — keeping it hidden, allowing it to grow away from prying eyes. Jeremiah 17:11 uses this image: one who "covers eggs that he has not laid" accumulates dishonest wealth, as if he were jealously guarding it, but it will escape him.
H1716.origine: The Hebrew verb dāgār comes from a root that evokes the idea of gathering and covering. The word is linked to the animal instinct of protecting offspring. It is a rare verb that captures the powerful image of a mother surrounding and preserving her eggs or young — an image of warmth, care, and secret growth.
H1716.emploi: The verb dāgār appears twice in the Hebrew Bible, both times in the prophets. In Isaiah 34:15, it describes the serpent covering its eggs in desolate ruins — it is nature persisting after destruction. In Jeremiah 17:11, Jeremiah uses it in a parable: the man who accumulates wealth unjustly is like a partridge that covers eggs she has not laid — he possesses them, certainly, but not legitimately, and they will not last. In both cases, the word charges the concrete image with moral or prophetic depth.
H1716.portee: To cover speaks of what is hidden, grows slowly, and cannot be held for long. For the reader, Jeremiah 17:11 invites reflection: injustice may seem lucrative for a time, but it has no legitimate roots and will collapse. The word reminds us that true wealth, like offspring, must be born justly to endure.

sens: Part of the female body, the breast or mammary gland
Chest or entire body taken as an object of desire
Charm, physical attractiveness
H1717.detail:
1. The word refers to the breast or mammary gland of the female body: it is the physical organ. Ezekiel 23:3 speaks of the "virgin breast" of a woman abused in Egypt, and verse 21 mentions the Egyptians who pressed the "mammaries" as a sign of domination and abuse.

2. By extension, the word can evoke the chest or the female body as a whole, as an object of desire or manifestation of youth. Ezekiel 23:8 describes how the Egyptians "had touched her virgin breast" — an act that mingles youth, vulnerability, and carnal desire.

3. The term also takes on a figurative sense of charm or physical attractiveness. In Proverbs 5:19, the translation uses "charms" to refer to what makes a woman alluring: "Be intoxicated always with her charms."
H1717.origine: The Hebrew root dad evokes the idea of sweetness and tenderness. The word belongs to the concrete vocabulary of the human body. It is specifically used for breasts or mammary glands, and this from the Old Testament onward. In biblical Hebrew, this word always refers to a physical reality or what proceeds from it (charm, attraction).
H1717.emploi: The word appears 4 times in the Old Testament, concentrated in two very different contexts: Proverbs and Ezekiel. In Proverbs 5:19, it is rendered as "charms" and is part of an appeal to marital fidelity — the beloved woman must constantly captivate her husband with her charm. In the three uses in Ezekiel 23, the term takes on a dark tone: it designates the breast or mammaries in scenes of prostitution and sexual abuse in Egypt. The contrast is striking: on one side, the healthy attraction at the heart of marriage; on the other, the vulnerability exploited by debauchery.
H1717.portee: This word invites the reader to consider two realities of physical attraction: one, beautiful and legitimate within marriage, where the wonder of the spouse is blessed; the other, destructive, where the body becomes an object of exploitation. It reminds us that marital love, far from being shameful, is a gift from God to celebrate, while unbridled lust leads to ruin.

sens: to walk with a deliberate and measured pace
to progress step by step
to move forward with gravity or humility
H1718.detail:
1. Advance slowly describes the act of moving by walking, but not in haste — it is a thoughtful, almost solemn gait. In Psalms 42:5, the psalmist remembers the time when he "advanced" at the head of the crowd toward the temple amid shouts of joy: it is a voluntary, composed progression that marks both a clear intention and a certain majesty.
2. Progressing step by step emphasizes the deliberate nature of the movement, as if each step is carefully considered. This contrasts with fleeing or rushing: one moves forward, but without haste, with a kind of measured dignity.
3. Moving forward with gravity or humility denotes a gait that expresses a certain inner attitude. In Isaiah 38:15, Hezekiah asserts that he will "walk humbly" for the rest of his days after his trial: the verb characterizes a life lived with a serious attitude, aware of human fragility.
H1718.origine: The Hebrew verb דָּדָה comes from a root that expresses the idea of walking or moving gradually, without haste. The fundamental meaning is that of slow and deliberate progression, like someone who measures their steps. This image of slow walking permeates all biblical uses of the term.
H1718.emploi: This verb appears only twice in the Bible, both in contexts of melancholy or gravity. In Psalms 42:5, the exiled psalmist joyfully remembers his solemn walk toward the temple. In Isaiah 38:15, Hezekiah, healed from his deadly illness, declares that he will now walk humbly all his days, marked by the awareness of his mortality. In both cases, the verb paints a gait that is neither hurried nor careless, but conscious and collected.
H1718.portee: This word invites reflection on how one walks through life. It reminds us that biblical faith is not about rushing foolishly, but about moving forward with intention and seriousness, aware of the realities of time and our fragility. For Hezekiah, this new humility in his walk is the fruit of trial and salvation: it expresses a lasting inner transformation.

sens: Region of Southern Arabia
People of Arab traders
Center of trade exchanges
H1719A.detail: Dedan is a region and a people of Southern Arabia, likely located in the lowlands of this desert region. It is mentioned alongside Tema (Jeremiah 25:23 and Ezekiel 25:13), another Arabian region. The Dedanites are portrayed as active traders: they traded with Tyre, the great port city, providing horse blankets and participating in extensive trade networks (Ezekiel 27:15 and 27:20). At the time of prophetic judgments, Dedan is among the nations that will be affected by the Lord's punishments or that will wonder, astonished, how calamity could strike (Ezekiel 38:13).
H1719A.origine: The Hebrew name Dedan designates a region and its people. It also appears in the form "Dedanites" (Dedani, H1720) to refer to the inhabitants. In biblical geography, Dedan is associated with other desert peoples of Arabia, forming a community of traders in the southeastern Arabian Peninsula.
H1719A.emploi: Dedan is mentioned six times in the Old Testament, always in the prophetic books (Jeremiah and Ezekiel). It first appears among the nations that will be judged by the Lord (Jeremiah 25:23). In Jeremiah 49:8, Dedan is threatened with calamity and invited to flee. Ezekiel geographically situates it (from the territory of Edom, 25:13) and primarily describes it as an important commercial power, a partner of Tyre in international trade (27:15 and 27:20). Finally, in Ezekiel 38:13, Dedan is among those who question the chief of Magog about his belligerent intentions. These uses show that Dedan was a prosperous and influential region of Arab trade, well-known in biblical times.
H1719A.portee: Dedan reminds us that the God of Israel reigns over all nations, including the distant desert peoples whose names are barely known today. The prophets proclaim His judgment to the ends of the known world, showing that no one escapes His sovereignty. These texts invite the reader to see divine providence at work far beyond the borders of Israel.

sens: Descendant of Cush, son of Raamah
People or region trading with the ancient world
H1719B.detail:
1. Dedan is a man from the family of Cush (ancient Ethiopia), son of Raamah and brother of Sheba, mentioned in the genealogy of nations at the beginning of the Bible (Genesis 10:7 and 1 Chronicles 1:9). He represents an eponymous ancestor, meaning that his name also designates the people or region that descends from him.
2. By extension, Dedan designates a people or a trading region of the ancient world, likely located in Southern Arabia or Northeast Africa, known for its exchanges with neighboring nations.
H1719B.origine: The name Dedan means "low country" or "low region" in Hebrew, perhaps suggesting the coastal or hilly geography of the territory. It is an ethnic name formed according to biblical custom: the eponymous founder gives his name to all his descendants and to his territory.
H1719B.emploi: Dedan appears only twice in the canonical Bible, in two parallel passages that list the descendants of Cush after the flood (Genesis 10:7 and 1 Chronicles 1:9). In these genealogical lists, he is identified as the son of Raamah and brother of Sheba, within the great dispersion of peoples. Although mentioned only in these two verses, Dedan is linked to a group of southern and eastern peoples known for trade: this suggests a people active in the commercial exchanges of antiquity.

sens: son of Jokshan in the time of the Patriarchs
eponymous ancestor of a people in the Middle East
H1719C.detail:
1. Dedan is a son of Jokshan, himself a son of Abraham and his concubine Keturah. He appears in the genealogy of Abraham's descendants listed in Genesis 25:3 and 1 Chronicles 1:32.
2. The name Dedan has given its name to a people or region: his three sons, Ashurim, Letushim, and Leummim, found the lineages that will carry his memory and mark. This practice was common in antiquity, where the fathers of lineages gave their name to their descendants collectively.
H1719C.origine: The name Dedan means "low country" or "low region" in Hebrew, which perhaps evokes the geography of the area where this people settled. The name belongs to the family of Abraham's descendants listed in chapter 25 of Genesis, which traces the origins of the peoples surrounding Israel.
H1719C.emploi: Dedan is mentioned only twice in the Bible, both in genealogical lists. In Genesis 25:3, he is included in the enumeration of Jokshan's children, whom Abraham had by his concubine Keturah after the death of Sarah. The text also mentions his three sons, indicating that Dedan fathered a lineage that established itself as a distinct people. In 1 Chronicles 1:32, the same genealogy is repeated, confirming the importance of this lineage in Israel's historical memory. These genealogies situate Dedan and his descendants in the context of the neighboring peoples of Israel in the Middle East.

sens: Region in the northwest of Arabia
Inhabitants or merchants from this region
H1720.detail: 1. Dedan refers to a region located in the northwest of Arabia, a lowland or plain area (the name literally means "lowland"). It is a populated and organized area, known for its active inhabitants and merchant caravans. 2. The word can also refer to the inhabitants themselves or the merchant caravans originating from Dedan. In Isaiah 21:13, the prophet addresses the caravans of Dedan passing through Arabia: these are men accustomed to traveling, trading, exposed to the insecurity and troubles that the prophet announces.
H1720.origine: Dedan is an ancient Semitic place name, attested in the Old Testament. Its name means "lowland" or "low region," which describes the geography of this Arabian area. It is a commercial and inhabited center, linked to the trade routes of the ancient Near East.
H1720.emploi: Dedan appears a few times in the Bible, particularly in the prophecies concerning Arabia and the neighboring nations of Israel. Isaiah 21:13 mentions the caravans of Dedan fleeing the calamities announced by the prophet, presenting them as travelers facing God's judgments. Thus, Dedan symbolizes a prosperous but vulnerable region, integrated into the prophetic judgment on foreign peoples.

sens: People descended from Dodan, son of Javan
Inhabitants of the islands and coasts of the eastern Mediterranean
Sea peoples and merchants of ancient times
H1721.detail: 1. The Dodanim are a people mentioned in the genealogy of the descendants of Noah: they descend from Javan, son of Japheth (Genesis 10:4). They are also referred to as Rodanim in 1 Chronicles 1:7, indicating that these two names refer to the same people. 2. This people is associated with other maritime peoples: Elishah, Tarshish, and Kittim. This suggests that they are populations living on the coasts and islands of the Mediterranean, engaged in navigation and trade. 3. Their name means "leaders" or "chiefs," which evokes the authority and importance of these peoples in the commercial and political network of ancient Mediterranean society.
H1721.origine: The name Dodanim (or Rodanim) comes from the Hebrew root meaning "leader" or "one who commands." The two forms of the name — Dodanim and Rodanim — appear in the two parallel passages of the Bible: one in Genesis and the other in 1 Chronicles, indicating a textual or dialectal variation of the same name. This people is classified among the descendants of Javan, who himself is a son of Japheth and ancestor of the Greek and Mediterranean peoples according to the biblical genealogy.
H1721.emploi: The Dodanim are mentioned only twice in the Bible: in Genesis 10:4 and in 1 Chronicles 1:7. These two passages are parallel and are part of the table of nations, which lists the descendants of Noah and populates the earth after the flood. The Dodanim are presented as one of the four sons of Javan, alongside Elishah, Tarshish, and Kittim. This position in the genealogy underscores their importance in the settlement of the eastern Mediterranean and their role as a people of navigators and merchants in antiquity.
H1721.portee: This mention of the Dodanim reminds us that God populated the earth in an orderly and intentional manner after the flood. It also shows that Scripture is concerned with distant peoples and foreign cultures, placing them within God's divine plan for history. For the believer, this emphasizes the universality of God's authority over all nations and peoples, from the nearest to the farthest.

sens: The precious yellow metal, bright and unalterable, highly sought after for its rarity and value
Objects, vessels, or adornments made of gold
Figuratively, that which is of great value, which holds supreme importance or particular dignity
H1722.detail: 1. The word refers to gold in its raw or worked form. It is an element of wealth and prestige: King Nebuchadnezzar has a massive gold statue made (Daniel 3:1), and the gold vessels of the Jerusalem temple, plundered during the conquest, are mentioned in Ezra 5:14 and 6:5, showing the importance of these precious objects. 2. The word is also used to refer to objects made of gold: the gold vessels of the temple, royal adornments. Belshazzar drinks from the gold vessels of the Jerusalem temple (Daniel 5:2-3) — an act of desecration that sullies these sacred objects. 3. In Nebuchadnezzar's vision, gold represents the highest degree of value and power: the head of gold of the great statue symbolizes his empire, the first and most glorious (Daniel 2:32, 2:38). Thus, gold becomes the image of what is eternal, preeminent, or unalterable.
H1722.origine: This is the Aramaic word for "gold" (the language spoken in Babylon and Aram). It corresponds to the Hebrew word זָהָב (zahav) from the Hebrew Old Testament. The word denotes the metal in its very nature: bright, indestructible, impervious to rust. In both Hebrew and Aramaic, it is a very ancient word, likely related to the idea of something that shines or stands out.
H1722.emploi: This word appears 23 times in the Aramaic parts of the Bible, concentrated in the books of Ezra and Daniel. It primarily denotes the material wealth of the Jerusalem temple: the gold vessels that were taken to Babylon are mentioned as treasures to be restored (Ezra 5:14, 6:5, 7:15-18). In the book of Daniel, the word is notably used for the gold statue commanded by Nebuchadnezzar (Daniel 3) and for the sacred vessels that Belshazzar profanes (Daniel 5). Gold symbolizes not only wealth but also royal power and the greatness of empires. In the prophetic vision of the statue (Daniel 2:32-45), gold represents the Babylonian empire itself, the first and most excellent of kingdoms.
H1722.portee: This word reminds the believer that material wealth, although impressive in the eyes of men, is never the lasting foundation of power or security. The great gold statue that Nebuchadnezzar commands to be worshiped stands in stark contrast to the integrity of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, who refuse to bow down (Daniel 3). Gold, magnificent yet fragile before God, invites us to set our hearts on what endures and cannot be destroyed — the divine word and justice.

sens: People or group mentioned in the official correspondence of the Persian empire
H1723.detail: 1. The Dehavites are a people mentioned only once in the Bible, in Ezra 4:9, in a letter that adversaries of the Jews send to King Artaxerxes of Persia. They are listed alongside other peoples of the empire to lend weight to their request: "The judges, governors, magistrates, stewards, and all other officers, both the Dehavites and the Apharsathkites, the Tarpelites, the Apharsites, the Archites, the Babylonians, the Susanchites, the Dehavites, and the Elamites..." This mention suggests that they are a group established in the Persian empire, likely colonists or administrators involved in the administrative life of the province beyond the River, in Syria.
H1723.origine: The name "Dehavites" could be related to a root meaning "sickly" (ill, weak), although the exact origin remains uncertain. It is likely a designation of Persian or Persian-Aramaic origin, given the entirely administrative and official context of the only verse where this name appears. This mention is found in Aramaic documents related to the Persian empire, indicating that this people or group was recognized as an administrative entity of the empire.
H1723.emploi: The Dehavites are mentioned only once in Ezra 4:9, in the context of the reconstruction of the Jerusalem temple under the reign of Darius. Persian officials and other peoples, including the Dehavites, seek to halt the reconstruction work. This group appears among a list of mixed peoples of the Persian empire, likely inhabitants or administrators from various regions. The mention remains brief and provides no additional details about their history, geographical origin, or specific role beyond this opposition to the reconstruction of the temple.

sens: To be struck with astonishment, seized with wonder
To be paralyzed, unable to act due to shock or surprise
H1724.detail:
1. The word describes the state of one who is struck with astonishment, like a blow that renders them immobile and mute with wonder. It is the experience of shock, of surprise that seizes the whole being. In Jeremiah 14:9, the prophet asks God: "Why would you be like a man stunned?", imagining a God seized with astonishment in the face of His people's misfortune, unable to react.
2. The word also implies a sense of helplessness: to be stunned is to be paralyzed, deprived of one's strength and ability to act. The stunned man cannot help anyone; he is like frozen by the shock. That is why Jeremiah adds: "like a hero unable to save us" — astonishment even robs the strongest of their power.
H1724.origine: The Hebrew verb דָּהַם (daham) expresses the idea of being disoriented, troubled in one's being. The root evokes the violent emotion that paralyzes. The word appears in the niphal form, which emphasizes a state that is experienced: one is not stunned by a voluntary act, but finds oneself seized, overwhelmed by astonishment. It is a passion that masters us.
H1724.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Jeremiah 14:9. The prophet uses it in a prayer of lament, where he addresses God in a moment of national crisis. The image is striking: Jeremiah imagines God Himself becoming "stunned", that is, paralyzed, unable to save His people. It is a dramatic way of expressing the apparent absence of God in the face of suffering. The prophet wants to awaken God, to remind Him of His identity and His commitment to Israel.
H1724.portee: This word helps us recognize within ourselves the experience of spiritual astonishment: those moments when suffering paralyzes us and we ask God why He seems inactive. Jeremiah does not deny that God may seem absent; he articulates it starkly to call for repentance and restoration. It is an honest prayer that acknowledges the mystery of God's silence in distress.

sens: To move quickly on horseback, at a gallop
To make noise while rushing forward with force
To rush, to charge with impetuosity
H1725.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes the gallop of a horse, this rapid and powerful movement where the animal charges forward. It is the concrete image: in Nahum 3:2, the prophet describes the noise of war, and among the sounds of battle, he mentions "the gallop of horses", these creatures that prance at full speed with a deafening noise.
2. By extension, the word evokes anything that rushes forward noisily and violently. The same verse also speaks of the "rumbling of chariots": it is this same idea of impetuous movement that produces a terrible crash, worthy of an army's charge.
3. Figuratively, "to gallop" can express momentum, impetuosity, action that charges straight ahead. It is the opposite of hesitation or measured steps.
H1725.origine: The Hebrew verb gahár expresses the image of a creature or object rushing forward with force. The root evokes the noise and speed of movement. It is mostly found in poetry and in the war narratives of the Bible, where it paints the vehemence of battles.
H1725.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Nahum 3:2. This prophetic book describes the ruin of Nineveh, the Assyrian capital, with striking images of battle and destruction. The prophet enumerates the terrifying sounds that precede the arrival of the enemy: the whip of battle, the rumbling of wheels, and the gallop of horses. Nahum uses this verb to create an atmosphere of dread and chaos, where everything rushes into turmoil.
H1725.portee: This word helps us understand how the Bible describes war: not as a distant event, but as something alive, noisy, threatening, that comes upon you. The image of the gallop of horses reminds us that military power, even overwhelming, is subject to God's judgment. For the reader of Nahum, hearing this gallop is to hear the divine judgment approaching against Assyrian oppression.

sens: Rapid and disorderly run to escape
Noise of galloping, clamor of horses in disarray
Movement of military rout
H1726.detail:
1. The word first describes a rapid and chaotic flight, one that saves lives by breaking ranks — the image of a troop that has only one thought: to leave as quickly as possible. In Judges 5:22, during the battle of Taanach, the hooves of the horses "resound" at the hasty flight of the enemy warriors: one hears the thunder of their hooves striking the ground, a sign of chaos and rout.
2. It is also the noise itself, the clamor produced by this panicked movement — the horses gallop, resonate, and this crash conveys the desperate urgency of the one who flees.
3. On a military level, this flight embodies total defeat: the enemy is no longer an organized army, but a multitude in disarray, where each one thinks only of saving their skin.
H1726.origine: The word comes from a root that expresses the idea of rushing, running with impetuosity. The initial image is that of violent and rapid movement, notably the gallop of horses resonating on hard ground. It is a rare word in Hebrew, used to make concrete and vivid the tumult of flight.
H1726.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Judges 5:22, in the famous Song of Deborah that celebrates Israel's victory over Sisera. This passage describes how the enemies, routed by God, flee in total confusion: one literally hears the crash of their fleeing horses. The context is that of a divine intervention that breaks the opposing army and transforms it into a panicked crowd.
H1726.portee: This word reminds us that true victory does not come from human military strength, but from God's intervention. The hasty flight of the enemy is not just a tactical defeat: it is a sign that God fights for His people and overturns those who oppose Him. For the believer, this image of enemy rout speaks of the certainty that God triumphs over evil, even when everything seems lost.

sens: To wither physically, to lose strength and vitality
To suffer from an ailment that slowly consumes
To be weighed down by grief or anxiety
H1727.detail:
1. Languish means to wither, to weaken gradually until completely losing one's strength. It is the image of a life that slowly fades away. In Leviticus 26:16, God announces that He will send fever that will make the eyes "languish" — the sick person loses their brightness, their gaze becomes dull, as if emptied of life.
2. The word describes a suffering that gnaws from within, that progressively consumes body and soul. In the same verse, it is said that the soul will be "suffering", consumed by illness and misfortune.
3. Beyond the body, languish can express moral anguish: it is the overwhelming of the heart that loses hope under the weight of misfortunes.
H1727.origine: The Hebrew root דּוּב (duv) fundamentally evokes the idea of drying up, withering, like a plant lacking water or a body weakened by illness. It expresses the image of a life that gradually fades away, not suddenly. The word belongs to the family of biblical terms that describe wear and the diminishing of strength.
H1727.emploi: The verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Leviticus 26:16, in the context of the curses that God promises to Israel if they transgress His covenant. There, languish describes one of the concrete punishments: the illness (fever and consumption) that weakens the people and their gaze. It is a stark term that stages the physical and visible punishment of unfaithfulness.
H1727.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that distancing from God has real and tangible consequences, not just spiritual ones. It invites us not to take our covenant with the Lord lightly. At the same time, languishing in the Hebrew Bible is never without hope: these threats are given to push the people toward repentance and return to God.

sens: one who captures fish for sustenance or commerce
one who casts or sets nets on the surface of the water
H1728.detail:
1. The fisherman is a man whose profession is to catch fish for sale or consumption. In Ezekiel 47:10, fishermen stand on the banks of the river to spread their nets and catch fish in abundance — this is the classic image of the water worker who lives by his skill and tools.
2. The term also evokes the action itself: one who casts nets, who stands near the water and earns his living from these daily repeated gestures. It is a humble yet recognized profession, requiring knowledge of the waters, seasons, and fish behavior.
H1728.origine: The Hebrew word דַּוָּג (davvag) comes from a root (דוג dag) meaning "fish"; the fisherman is literally "one of the fish" or "one who makes fish." This type of formation — adding a suffix to the name of a creature or thing to form the corresponding profession — is common in Hebrew. The word thus expresses a direct and natural relationship between man and his element: the fisherman belongs to the world of fish.
H1728.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Ezekiel 47:10, a vision passage where Ezekiel describes the healing waters that will flow from the Temple. It is a concrete and realistic usage: the fishermen are depicted as ordinary men who will practice their trade on this new river, casting their nets to capture a profusion of fish of all kinds. The image contrasts with the supernatural character of the context (water flowing from the sanctuary), grounding this wonder in a peaceful and productive scene of ordinary human life.
H1728.portee: This passage invites us to see that God's vision for restoration does not reject human labor or modest professions: the fisherman finds his natural place in the renewed world. It reminds us that all honest labor, even that of the humblest, has dignity and remains alive in God's plan.

sens: Curved hook for catching fish on a line
By extension, any sharp or pointed instrument that catches and wounds
That which attracts and holds someone against their will
H1729.detail: 1. The word primarily refers to a simple hook, the small curved piece placed at the end of a fishing line and baited to catch fish — this is its most concrete and literal meaning. 2. It can more broadly refer to any sharp or pointed object that catches and pierces, such as hooks or harpoons used to capture or wound. 3. Finally, it symbolizes what traps someone, attracting and holding them against their will: in Amos 4:2, the Lord threatens to take His people "with hooks," an image of brutal and humiliating judgment where the unbelieving Israelites will be carried away like fish caught in a trap.
H1729.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the action of hooking or piercing. It is a concrete term from daily life: fishing was a common activity in Israel and Judah, especially near the Sea of Galilee and the Jordan River. The image of the hook that catches and pulls has naturally extended to the realm of divine judgment and captivity.
H1729.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Amos 4:2. The prophet Amos denounces the oppression of the poor by the rich in Israel; the Lord swears to avenge this injustice by taking the people away with hooks — a violent image of capture and deportation. The context shows that this judgment will strike women as prey delivered into the hands of the enemy.
H1729.portee: This image of the hook reminds us that divine judgment is not abstract: it is concrete, personal, and reaches those who oppress. It also invites the reader to consider what "hooks" them — what temptations or sins keep them captive like a fish on a line — and to seek freedom in Jesus.

sens: person loved with tenderness and affection
object of deep desire and attachment
one towards whom love is directed
H1730G.detail:
1. The beloved is one who is deeply loved, one towards whom tenderness and affection are shown. It is the person who occupies a privileged place in the heart of the speaker. In Song of Solomon 1:13, the woman speaks of her beloved as a sachet of myrrh resting on her heart, showing how the one loved becomes like a precious object that one desires to keep close. 
2. The beloved also designates the object of deep desire and attachment: it is one who is sought after, desired to be seen and met. In Song of Solomon 2:8, the woman recognizes the voice of her beloved coming towards her, leaping on the mountains — an image of someone awaited with impatience and joy. 
3. By extension, the term expresses the idea of mutual possession and union: "I am my beloved's, and my beloved is mine" (Song of Solomon 6:3). It is a relationship of reciprocal belonging, where each belongs to the other.
H1730G.origine: The word dod comes from a root that expresses the idea of affection and tenderness. It is a word specifically used to designate one who is loved: the beloved, one who is the object of passionate or tender love. The same word can also refer to an uncle (paternal or maternal), as the familial bond that unites us to our uncle is also a bond of natural affection. This diversity of meanings shares a common root: the idea of affectionate closeness.
H1730G.emploi: This word appears 27 times in the Bible, almost exclusively in the Song of Solomon, this love poem that celebrates the romantic relationship between a man and a woman. It is constantly used by one of the two lovers to speak of the other: the woman speaks of "my beloved" and the man of "his beloved." The word always expresses a feeling of personal, intimate, and passionate love. In this poetic context, the beloved is described with admiration (Song of Solomon 5:10: "white and ruddy"), awaited with impatience, desired, and finally possessed in a mutual union. It is a language of tenderness and deep attachment.
H1730G.portee: For the Christian reader, this word illuminates how the Bible speaks of marital love as sincere, passionate, and mutual. Although it is a poetic text about earthly love, the Song of Solomon has also been read as an image of God's love for His people, or of Christ for the Church. This word reminds us that God desires a relationship of true affection with us, where we are precious and loved like the beloved in this poem — with tenderness, constancy, and joy.

sens: Deep and tender affection for someone, especially between lovers
Beloved, loved one
Uncle, brother of the father or mother
Passionate impulse, pleasure
H1730H.detail:
1. Love is the affection one has for someone, particularly conjugal or romantic love. It is the feeling that makes two beings desire and cherish each other: "How delightful is your love, my sister, my bride!" (Song of Solomon 4:10). This word designates the feeling itself, this attachment of the heart.
2. By extension, the word also refers to the loved one themselves, the one who is the object of this love: the beloved. That is why one can say "your love" to refer to the one whom one loves.
3. The word can also mean uncle — the brother of a parent — but this meaning is rare in the provided usages and likely comes from a different root.
4. In a passionate context, the word evokes the intoxication and pleasure that love brings: "Let us be intoxicated with love until morning" (Proverbs 7:18). It is the impulse and pleasure of surrendering to affection.
H1730H.origine: The Hebrew word dod comes from a root that expresses the idea of being dear, of being esteemed. It is related to other words denoting affection or esteem. In Greek, it is often rendered by agapé (love) or éros (desire) depending on the context. The word evokes both intimate tenderness and sincere esteem for the one whom we cherish.
H1730H.emploi: This word appears about 9 times in the Hebrew Bible, almost exclusively in the Song of Solomon and prophetic passages speaking of the love between God and Israel. The Song of Solomon uses it extensively to describe the passionate and tender love between the husband and wife: in Song of Solomon 1:2, 1:4, 4:10, 5:1, and 7:13, it constantly returns to speak of this mutual love that is better than wine and fills the heart with joy. In Proverbs 7:18, it takes on a sensual and carnal hue. The prophetic passages (Isaiah 5:1, Ezekiel 16:8, 23:17) use it symbolically to describe God's relationships with His people or Israel's unfaithfulness. The meaning thus varies from tender and pure feeling to carnal passion, depending on the context.
H1730H.portee: This word reminds believers that love is at the heart of human life and the relationship with God. The Song of Solomon celebrates conjugal love as a sacred good, a joy that God approves. The prophets also use it to show the personal and passionate love that God has for His people, inviting them to respond to this love with the same abandonment and tenderness.

sens: The brother of the father or mother
Relative of the previous generation, often with an affectionate or protective relationship
H1730I.detail: 1. The word primarily designates the brother of the father or mother — a direct kinship link recognized by law. Moses calls Mishael and Elzaphan, sons of Uziel, "uncles" of Aaron in Leviticus 10:4, because Uziel was the brother of Amram, Aaron's father. This relationship carries rights and duties: an uncle can redeem a needy relative (Leviticus 25:49) or inherit their property (Jeremiah 32:7-9, where Jeremiah buys the field of his uncle Hanamel). 2. Beyond the legal link, the word carries a nuance of affection and closeness — an uncle is often one who protects, who raises orphans (Mordecai raises Esther, his "daughter," but also his cousin, in Esther 2:7), or who advises with authority (Saul's uncle questions him informally in 1 Samuel 10:14-16).
H1730I.origine: The Hebrew root דּוּד (dud) or דּוֹד (dod) evokes the idea of one who loves or is loved — the word carries with it an affectionate warmth. In the family, the uncle is not a distant stranger, but a dear relative, often called to play a role of support or benevolent authority among the younger ones. The word is also used, in its root, to express love or tenderness.
H1730I.emploi: The word appears seventeen times in the Hebrew Bible, almost always in the strict sense: the uncle as a relative of the previous generation. It appears mainly in the legal narratives of the Law (Leviticus), where the uncle's relationship involves duties of redemption or succession (Leviticus 20:20, 25:49, Numbers 36:11). It is also found in royal stories (Saul and his uncle, Jehoiachin and Mattaniah in 2 Kings 24:17) and in the story of Esther (Mordecai as a father figure). Jeremiah himself buys the field of his uncle (Jeremiah 32:7-12), showcasing this kinship relationship in a symbolic prophetic act.
H1730I.portee: The uncle embodies the bond of family solidarity in the Bible: he is the one to count on when one has lost their parents (like Esther), or who has the right and duty to intervene in the succession or redemption of a relative in difficulty. This word reminds us that the faith of Israel rests on concrete family ties, woven by blood and affection, where everyone has a responsibility towards their own.

sens: Cooking container for cooking or serving
Basket for carrying or storing items
Closed object that can contain or receive something
H1731.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a pot or cooking cauldron, used for cooking food. In 1 Samuel 2:14, during the sacrifices at Shiloh, the priest plunges a fork into the cauldron to take his share of meat. It is a common household utensil, made of clay or metal.
2. It also refers to a basket or container used to carry, store, or preserve items. In 2 Kings 10:7, the heads of the kings are placed in baskets for transport. In Jeremiah 24:1, the prophet sees two baskets of figs before the temple, symbols of divine judgment.
3. More broadly, it is any container capable of holding something — whether for cooking, transport, or storage. In Job 41:11, the boiling pit of Leviathan evokes a burning vessel, a poetic image of destructive power.
H1731.origine: The Hebrew word דּוּד comes from a root expressing the idea of containment and closure. It has a common root with the word meaning "to love" (which etymologically could express a relationship of intimacy), but in this context, it simply designates a hollow and closed object. The word belongs to the domestic and artisanal vocabulary of ancient Israel.
H1731.emploi: This word appears 7 times in the Old Testament, mainly in contexts of cooking, worship, or prophecy. It is used for the cauldrons of sacrifices (1 Samuel 2:14; 2 Chronicles 35:13), transport baskets (2 Kings 10:7; Psalms 81:7), preservation baskets (Jeremiah 24:1-2), and poetic images (Job 41:11). The word does not change its fundamental meaning: it is always a hollow object serving to contain. The Segond translates this word with several French terms — basket, cauldron, container, vessel — depending on the context, but it is the same Hebrew word.
H1731.portee: This word reminds us that God sees and blesses the everyday acts of service, work, and cooking. Ordinary utensils — baskets, cauldrons — become witnesses of divine faithfulness. In Jeremiah 24, the two baskets of figs are a parable of judgment: the most mundane object becomes the means by which God speaks of His plan for His people. It is a lesson that nothing in ordinary life escapes the Lord's attention.

sens: the youngest son of Jesse
king of Israel after Saul
man of war and victor over Goliath
author of psalms and musician
ancestor of the Messiah
H1732.detail:
1. David is first presented as the youngest son of Jesse, a man from the tribe of Judah (Ruth 4:17). He becomes a shepherd, tending his father's flocks before being called to a greater destiny.
2. He is anointed king by Samuel and becomes the second king of Israel, succeeding Saul (1 Samuel 16:13). His reign marks the beginning of what the Bible calls the "united monarchy."
