3. He makes a name for himself by killing the giant Goliath with a sling and a stone, which makes him famous among the people (1 Samuel 17). This victory brings him closer to King Saul, where he becomes a court musician.
4. David is a musician and poet: he plays the harp to soothe Saul and composes many psalms that will be recited in the worship of Israel (1 Chronicles 15:16).
5. He is the starting point of the messianic promise: God promises that the Messiah will come from his lineage and that his throne will last forever (2 Samuel 7).
H1732.origine: The name David means "beloved" in Hebrew. It comes from a root that expresses affection and tenderness. David bears this name which reveals both his personal character and God's favor upon his life.
H1732.emploi: David appears more than 900 times in the Bible, primarily in the books of Samuel, Kings, and Chronicles. He is first an unknown young shepherd, son of Jesse (Ruth 4:17 and 1 Samuel 16), then becomes the trusted man of King Saul as a musician and warrior (1 Samuel 16:19-23). His military exploits, notably his victory over Goliath (1 Samuel 17), make him a national hero. He will marry several women and have many sons, including Solomon who will succeed him. Throughout the historical books, David is presented as a warrior king, an organizer of worship, and a man after God's own heart, despite his personal failings.
H1732.portee: David embodies the leader that God chooses not based on appearance or brute strength, but according to the heart. His story teaches that God can use an unknown young man to accomplish great things. His dynastic promise announces messianic hope: the Messiah will come from David's lineage. For Christians, David is a key figure in the Old Testament that reveals both God's grace towards an imperfect man and the expectation of the eternal King who would be his descendant.

sens: Sister of the father or mother
Wife of the uncle (brother of the father or mother)
H1733.detail:
1. The aunt is the sister of the father or mother. Jochebed was the aunt of Amram, meaning she was the sister of his father or mother (Exodus 6:20).
2. The wife of the uncle, that is, the woman of the brother of the father or mother, is also called an aunt. This is why the Law prohibited relations with her: she was considered a very close relative, the same degree as a sister of the father (Leviticus 18:14 and 20:20).
H1733.origine: The Hebrew word דֹּדָה (dode-dah) is formed from the root דוד (dod), which designates the uncle or sister of the father/mother. This root expresses the idea of close kinship. The feminine דֹּדָה adds the feminine form to specifically designate the woman — either the sister or the wife of the brother.
H1733.emploi: The word appears three times in the Hebrew Bible, always to designate a close relative. In Exodus 6:20, it identifies Jochebed as the aunt of Amram (sister of his father or mother). In Leviticus 18:14 and 20:20, it refers to a legal prohibition: an Israelite was not to have intimate relations with the aunt (the wife of his uncle, the brother of his father), as she was ranked at the same level as other prohibited relatives. These three passages are all legislative or genealogical: the word always designates a first-degree relative by marriage or blood.
H1733.portee: The aunt, in the Law of Moses, reminds us that family is a sacred circle whose ties require reserve and chastity. The fact that the wife of the uncle is treated as an aunt by blood shows how the Law viewed marriage: not as a mere union between two individuals, but as an entry into kinship, a family. It is an invitation to respect the natural and sacred boundaries that protect family life.

sens: father of Pua, man of Issachar during the time of the Judges
H1734G.detail: Dodo is a man from the tribe of Issachar, ancestor of Tola who was a judge of Israel after Abimelech (Judges 10:1). He is known only through his son Pua, whose son Tola "rose to deliver Israel." His name means "his beloved."
H1734G.origine: The name Dodo means "his beloved" in Hebrew. It is a simple and affectionate name, borne in ancient Israel by at least three different men from successive generations.
H1734G.emploi: Dodo appears only once in the Bible, in Judges 10:1, where he is presented as the father of Pua and the grandfather of Tola, the judge of Israel. He lived during the time of the Judges and represents one of those generations known only through the genealogy of those who became prominent figures.

sens: Father of Eleazar, one of David's three elite warriors
H1734H.detail: Dodo is a warrior of Israel during the time of King David. He is best known as the father of Eleazar, who distinguished himself by an extraordinary feat: during a battle against the Philistines, while the men of Israel retreated, Eleazar held his ground and achieved a resounding victory alongside David (2 Samuel 23:9). Dodo himself, though less famous than his son, bears a name that means "his beloved," which highlights the honor of his lineage.
H1734H.origine: The name Dodo literally means "his beloved" in Hebrew. It comes from a root expressing affection and love. This patronymic was borne by several families in Israel, as shown by the two mentions in 1 Chronicles 27:4 (where Dodo is also called Dodai) and 1 Chronicles 11:12, which designate the father of Eleazar the Ahohite.
H1734H.emploi: Dodo appears twice in the lists of David's warriors: in 2 Samuel 23:9 and in 1 Chronicles 11:12. These two passages recount the same event and describe Eleazar, son of Dodo, as one of the three most important warriors who served David. Dodo is mentioned only by his relationship to his illustrious son; his own role is not detailed, but his name remains attached to the military glory of Eleazar and the memory of the heroes of the time of the United Monarchy.

sens: father of Elhanan, one of David's warriors
H1734I.detail: Dodo is a proper name designating the father of Elhanan, a renowned warrior in the service of King David. He appears in two passages that list the valiant men of the king: in 2 Samuel 23:24 and 1 Chronicles 11:26, where he is presented as originating from Bethlehem. His son Elhanan is counted among David's thirty elite warriors.
H1734I.origine: The name Dodo means "his beloved" in Hebrew, formed from a root that expresses love and affection. It is a common personal name in ancient Israel.
H1734I.emploi: Dodo appears only twice in the Bible, always to designate the father of Elhanan. In 2 Samuel 23:24, he is mentioned in the list of the thirty valiant warriors of King David; the same passage also appears in 1 Chronicles 11:26 with identical context. These two references are parallel and describe the same character and the same historical period — that of the united monarchy under David.

sens: Man of Judah mentioned only once in the Bible
Father of the prophet Eliezer who criticized King Jehoshaphat
H1735.detail: Dodava is a man from Mareshah, a city in Judah. He appears in the story only because his son, Eliezer, was a prophet and had the courage to confront King Jehoshaphat about a bad political alliance (2 Chronicles 20:37). Nothing else is known about his life or personal character.
H1735.origine: The name literally means "beloved of the Lord" in Hebrew. It combines two elements: love or affection, and the divine name. It was a name that expressed God's blessing or favor upon the one who bore it.
H1735.emploi: Dodava is mentioned only once in the entire Bible, in 2 Chronicles 20:37. He is known only as the father of Eliezer of Mareshah. This Eliezer was a man of God who received a prophetic message to confront King Jehoshaphat about his alliance with King Ahaziah of Israel. It is a discreet example of prophetic faithfulness during a time of division between the Northern and Southern kingdoms.
H1735.portee: Dodava reminds us that God raises up prophets in important moments of history, even among lesser-known men. His son Eliezer shows that one does not need to be a great figure to bear the word of God; what matters is faithfulness to the message received.

sens: Plant with tonic and aphrodisiac properties
Fruit or root of this plant
Symbol of fertility and carnal desire
H1736.detail:
1. The mandrake is a plant known for its stimulating properties, particularly regarding fertility and desire. It is a true Mediterranean plant, recognizable by its root that vaguely resembles a human figure and its small yellow fruits. In the account of Genesis 30, Reuben finds them in the fields at harvest time and brings them to his mother Leah, indicating that they were gathered for consumption.
2. Figuratively, the mandrake becomes an issue of intimate negotiation: Rachel exchanges a night with Jacob for these mandrakes with Leah (Genesis 30:15-16), revealing the credit given to this plant for promoting conception.
3. In the Song of Solomon (7:14), the mandrake symbolizes sensual delights and romantic passion: the lover enumerates the fruits of desire — the mandrakes spread their fragrance — as treasures she has kept for the one she loves, evoking both the enchanting scent and the intoxication of desire.
H1736.origine: The Hebrew word דּוּדַי (dudaïm) likely comes from a root denoting love or carnal desire, which exactly reflects the biblical usage: it is also called "love apple" in some traditions. The name already reveals the plant's reputation. It is a true plant of the ancient Near East, well-known and utilized.
H1736.emploi: The word appears only four times in the Bible, all in two foundational narratives: first in the marital drama of Jacob with Leah and Rachel (Genesis 30:14-16), where the mandrakes become the subject of a meaningful exchange regarding motherhood and the right to marital intimacy; then in the Song of Solomon (7:14), where they symbolize the delights of love. In these two contexts, the mandrake is linked to fertility, desire, and sensuality — rarely in a purely botanical sense, but always with an emotional and existential charge.
H1736.portee: This word invites the reader to see how the Bible speaks frankly about carnal realities — desire, fertility, marital rivalry — without avoidance or shame. It also shows the ancient wisdom of the people of Israel, who understood the resources of nature to comprehend and accept their own bodies. For the Christian couple, it is a reminder that the Bible does not condemn desire in marriage, but places it within God's plan for life and fertility.

sens: A military leader of Israel during the time of the united monarchy
H1737.detail: Dodaï is an officer who commanded the second division of King David's army, consisting of twenty-four thousand men. He is referred to as an "Ahohite," indicating his origin or family (1 Chronicles 27:4). This system of monthly divisions ensured a constant rotation of troops for the defense of the kingdom.
H1737.origine: The name Dodaï literally means "beloved" or "loving" in Hebrew, derived from the root meaning love or affection. It is closely related to the name Dodo (הדּוֹדוֹ), and Dodaï could be a variant or nickname. This type of name reflects a quality or sentiment that parents wished to associate with their child.
H1737.emploi: Dodaï appears only once in the Bible in 1 Chronicles 27:4, in the list of officers who commanded the twelve divisions of the royal army established by King David. Each division was responsible for one month of service. Dodaï commanded that of the second month and was assisted by a certain Mikloth. This mention places him among the important figures of David's military administration, although few additional details are given about his life or actions.
H1737.portee: The mention of Dodaï reminds us that David's reign was organized in a structured manner, with an effective military administration and trustworthy men in key positions. This illustrates how God granted wisdom to the king to organize his kingdom, and how obedience and military service were part of the national life of Israel.

sens: State of infirmity or discomfort related to menstruation
Ritual impurity associated with menstrual flow
H1738.detail:
1. The word designates the physical discomfort that a woman experiences during her menstruation — malaise, weakness — and by extension the menstrual state itself. In Leviticus 12:2, the woman who has given birth is "unclean as during her menstrual period," which shows that the Bible recognizes this state as a biological reality.
2. In Levitical legislation, this phenomenon results in ritual impurity: it lasts seven days and temporarily prohibits access to the sanctuary. This impurity is not a moral condemnation, but a category of the law of Israelite worship, akin to other situations declared impure.
H1738.origine: The Hebrew verb comes from a root that expresses weakness, illness, physical discomfort. It can apply to all kinds of infirmity, but in this context, it specifically designates the particular condition of menstruation. The word conveys a medical and physiological observation: the temporary weakening associated with this natural process.
H1738.emploi: The verb appears only once in the received Hebrew text: in Leviticus 12:2. It is used to describe the ritual condition of the woman after childbirth, which is treated in the same way as that of a woman during menstruation. This passage is part of the law of purity, which establishes the timeframes and conditions that women must observe after childbirth or during their periods before they can offer a sacrifice and resume their place in community life.
H1738.portee: This text shows that the Bible recognizes the biological realities of the female body without condemning them, while situating them within a religious framework of ritual purity. Understanding this vocabulary helps the modern reader see that the law of Moses was not disdainful, but a pedagogy that integrated the created order — including sexuality and reproduction — into worship and holiness.

sens: State of a woman during her menstrual period, source of legal impurity
Physical weakness, languor or debilitation of the body
Moral suffering, deep sadness of the soul
H1739.detail:
1. In Levitical law, this word refers to the state of menstruation in women, considered to create ritual impurity. It is a bodily reality linked to the natural cycle of the female body, which leads to prohibitions of contact and prescriptions for purification. In Leviticus 15:33 and 20:18, it is called "flow" or "disposition."
2. In a broader physical sense, the word describes weakness or debilitation of the body. In Lamentations 1:13, the prophet declares that a fire has been kindled in her bones and that she suffers from a "languor every day": the image is one of chronic fatigue, an exhaustion that weighs endlessly.
3. The word is also used for moral suffering, the burden of the soul. In Lamentations 5:17, "our heart is suffering" expresses not a physical illness, but a deep sorrow, a sadness that affects the whole being.
H1739.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root expressing the idea of languor, weakness, or debilitation. It primarily denotes a manifest bodily state — menstruation or flow — before extending to any form of physical weakness or inner suffering. The same family of words in Hebrew encompasses the general idea of being weakened, ill, or overwhelmed.
H1739.emploi: This word appears only five times in the Hebrew Bible. Three occurrences are found in Levitical law (Leviticus 15 and 20), where it designates menstrual impurity according to Israelite purity laws. Two occurrences are in the book of Lamentations, where it takes on a much broader meaning: that of a weakness or suffering that affects the whole body or soul. In Isaiah 30:22, a related form describes the defiled remnants of idols that will be scattered as impurity. The meaning thus evolves from the physiological to the spiritual: from the natural state of the body to the image of desolation and exhaustion.
H1739.portee: This word reminds the reader that the ancient Law took seriously the realities of the human body and its impact on communal life. For today's Christian, it invites reflection on how Jesus freed His people from these legal observances while revealing the dignity of the whole person, body and soul. The passages from Lamentations also show that suffering and affliction are real, and that the Bible speaks honestly about the exhaustion and disenchantment that believers go through.

sens: Rinse or clean something by passing it through water
Purify, remove a moral or spiritual stain
Expel, drive away, reject
H1740.detail:
1. The primary meaning is practical: to wash means to rinse something to remove it from water, to clean it. This is seen in Ezekiel 40:38, where there is a chamber intended for washing the burnt offerings, that is, rinsing the sacrificed animals. In 2 Chronicles 4:6, we find this sense of ritual cleaning in the temple.
2. Washing takes on a spiritual significance when God "purifies" Jerusalem from the blood that defiles the city (Isaiah 4:4). The image of rinsing with water becomes the image of removing evil, of moral stain. God washes to make pure.
3. In a stronger usage, to wash means to drive away, to expel: Jeremiah 51:34 speaks of a nation "driven away" from its land, carried off like a wave. The movement of rinsing becomes a brutal rejection.
H1740.origine: The Hebrew verb דּוּחַ comes from a root that evokes the movement of flowing water, rinsing, carrying away. The verbal form used in the Bible is the Hiphil ("to cause to rinse"), which reinforces the idea of action. The word belongs to the vocabulary of worship and ritual purification in Israel.
H1740.emploi: This verb appears four times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in the prophets and temple narratives. Isaiah uses it to describe the eschatological purification of Jerusalem by God. Ezekiel and 2 Chronicles use it in a cultic context: washing sacrifices before offering them. Jeremiah gives the verb a more brutal sense: to be washed also means to be expelled, carried away. The same word can thus mean to ritually clean or to violently chase away, depending on the context.
H1740.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that God does not merely forgive: He purifies, He removes the stain of sin as one would rinse away dirt. It is an image of radical transformation. It also teaches that God's justice acts forcefully: it leaves nothing of evil remaining, it drives it far away.

sens: physical repugnance for food
state of wasting or weakening of the body
feeling of nausea or deep fatigue
H1741.detail:
1. The word first describes an instinctive repugnance, a visceral disgust towards certain foods — like Job who cannot swallow his food because it repulses him (Job 6:7), as his affliction has made him unable to eat normally.
2. It also evokes the state of languor and physical wasting that accompanies illness: the body weakens, vitality fades, one loses all taste for life (Psalms 41:4).
3. More broadly, it designates this deep nausea, this fatigue of living that arises from prolonged suffering — not only physical but also moral, a sort of disenchantment with existence.
H1741.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that carries the idea of repulsion and languor. It is rare in the Bible, which shows that it names a very particular experience: not a simple illness, but the disgust and dejection it provokes. The root evokes something that "refuses," that resists — hence the double meaning: refusal to eat, refusal to live.
H1741.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. Job uses it to express his repugnant inability to nourish himself: his illness has affected him so much that food itself revolts him. In the Psalms, it designates the state of wasting of the sick person on his bed — not the illness itself, but this languor, this crushing of the whole being. The two occurrences converge: the word paints less the illness than the moral and physical state that follows it — this moment when the body refuses, when the soul fades away.
H1741.portee: This word helps the reader to name an often invisible experience: the deep decline that prolonged illness inflicts, far beyond physical pain. It validates those who suffer in this way, showing them that they are not alone in this existential disgust, and encourages them to cry out to God, as Job did, without shame.

sens: Afflicted, burdened by moral or physical pain
Exhausted, powerless in the face of grief
Wounded internally, the heart consumed by sadness
H1742.detail:
1. The word describes a state of deep suffering, often related to guilt or remorse: it is the heart that "suffers," bearing an invisible wound. In Isaiah 1:5, the prophet says that the entire nation is "suffering" from head to foot, like a sick person: the image is that of a moral illness caused by repeated rebellions against God.
2. The word also expresses emotional exhaustion in the face of persistent pain: the heart can no longer stand. Jeremiah declares in 8:18, "my heart suffers within me" — it is the fatigue of accumulated sorrow, weighing inside the chest like a burden.
3. It is a state of inner weakness caused by grief: not a moment of passing sadness, but a lasting despondency that makes one ill. In Lamentations 1:22, the groaning Jerusalem says that her heart is "suffering" — she is broken from within by her transgressions.
H1742.origine: The root fundamentally means "to be weak," "to fail." The word carries the idea of a force that flows out, of a vitality that is exhausted. The context of the three uses shows that this weakness particularly affects the heart, the seat of emotions and morale in the Bible. That is why the word is mainly applied to inner suffering, to moral depression rather than physical illness.
H1742.emploi: The word appears three times in biblical Hebrew, exclusively to qualify the state of the heart. In Isaiah 1:5, it paints the spiritual state of Israel pursued by punishments. In Jeremiah 8:18, it expresses the personal distress of the prophet who grieves for his people. In Lamentations 1:22, the besieged city itself describes itself as "suffering." In all cases, it is a term of intense moral suffering, often linked to guilt or mourning.
H1742.portee: This word invites us to recognize that the Bible does not hide moral suffering or emotional exhaustion. It names them, it validates them. For the reader, it is a permission to acknowledge when one's heart "suffers," burdened by the awareness of sin, loss, or the weight of responsibilities — and to express it before God. It is also a call to tenderness towards those whose hearts are wounded.

sens: To reduce to fine powder by striking forcefully in a mortar
To grind or crush something by pounding
H1743.detail:
1. To crush means to repeatedly and vigorously strike a solid substance with a pestle in a mortar to reduce it to fine powder or paste. The text in Numbers 11:8 gives a concrete image: the Israelites in the desert crushed the manna in a mortar to transform it into flour or powder before cooking it or making cakes. It is a classic domestic task, a way to prepare food or materials.
2. More broadly, to crush refers to any operation of grinding by percussion: to smash, to break, to transform a compact substance into finer particles. The action implies a repetition of blows and an appropriate instrument (pestle and mortar).
H1743.origine: The Hebrew verb dukh comes from a root that evokes the action of striking, hitting. It describes a very ancient and universal gesture: transforming matter by percussion. This word belongs to the domestic and culinary vocabulary of the ancient Near East.
H1743.emploi: The verb dukh appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Numbers 11:8. It describes the daily work of the Israelites who crushed the manna in the desert. This unique use clearly situates it in the practical context of food preparation: the pestle striking in the mortar to transform a raw food into flour or powder ready to be cooked.
H1743.portee: This word reminds us of God's extraordinary providence in the desert: the manna was not a ready-made food, but a raw material that required human effort. The Israelites had to crush it, cook it, prepare it — a lesson that God provides not by removing the effort from His people, but by giving them the material and the opportunity to work together. It is a revealing detail of concrete and laborious faith.

sens: Impure bird according to the law of Moses
Ground bird with a distinctive crest
H1744.detail:
1. The hoopoe is a bird that Israel considers impure and unfit for consumption. It appears in both lists of the Law that enumerate the birds to avoid: in Leviticus 11:19 and Deuteronomy 14:18, it is classified among other impure birds like the stork and the heron, without a precise reason given.
2. It is a terrestrial and migratory bird, recognizable by its distinctive crest on its head. This bird existed in the land of Israel and was well known to the Hebrews; it is not a mythical or exotic bird for them, but a familiar animal in their environment, a bird they saw in nature.
H1744.origine: The Hebrew word דּוּכִיפַת (dukiphat) designates this bird by a phonetic imitation of its characteristic cry, an onomatopoeia that recalls the sound "doup-doup-doup" that the hoopoe produces. This type of formation by imitation of natural sound is common in animal names in Hebrew, with the ancients speaking directly of the cry when naming the creature.
H1744.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, always in the legal lists of impure animals. These two occurrences — Leviticus 11 and Deuteronomy 14 — are parallel passages that repeat the same dietary prohibitions. The hoopoe is listed in a strictly legislative context, without narrative or particular trait: it is simply enumerated among the creatures that the people of Israel must reject to remain pure, in accordance with the Law. This classification as an impure bird may reflect Hebrew observations about its behavior or diet, but the Bible does not provide an explanation for it.
H1744.portee: For a Christian reader, the mention of the hoopoe reminds us that the Old Testament Law given to Moses covers all areas of life — including the most everyday, like the choice of what to eat. These lists show us the scope and detail of the divine will addressed to the people. Although Christians are no longer bound by these prohibitions (see Mark 7:19), they reveal the holiness required and the thought of God that presides over every detail.

sens: the total absence of noise or speech
the state of tranquility, peace without agitation
inactivity, immobility
death, the abode of the dead where silence reigns
the inability to praise God
H1745.detail:
1. Silence in the literal sense is the absence of noise and speech: it is the tranquility that prevails when nothing makes noise and when no one speaks.
2. It also denotes a state of peace and rest, free from troubles or tumult: a calm and unagitated situation.
3. It is also immobility and inactivity, the absence of movement or action.
4. In a more serious sense, silence is associated with death and the abode of the dead: in Psalms 94:17, if God did not come to the psalmist's aid, his soul would descend into the "abode of silence," that is, into death. In Psalms 115:17, the dead cannot praise the Lord because they are in the "place of silence."
5. The silence of death also means the total inability to praise God and to participate in the life of worship: the dead cannot cry, pray, or give thanks.
H1745.origine: The word "silence" comes from a Hebrew root that primarily evokes the absence of sound. In Hebrew, the same concept is expressed by this simple and direct root, without complicated derivation. The basic image is that of a voice that stops, a noise that ceases, a person who no longer speaks. In the Old Testament, this word is used to describe order and tranquility, but also to evoke death: the silence of the tomb, where no word resounds anymore.
H1745.emploi: The word "silence" appears twice in the Psalms, in both provided usages, and in both cases, it describes the abode of the dead. In Psalms 94:17, the psalmist says he would have descended into the "silence" if it had not been for God's help: silence here is synonymous with imminent death, disappearance. In Psalms 115:17, silence is presented as the characteristic of the place of the dead, in contrast to the living who can celebrate the name of the Lord. Silence is therefore never presented as something desirable: it is absence, powerlessness, death.
H1745.portee: For the Christian reader, these passages remind us how precious life is and how urgent God's help is: it is in the present life that we can praise, pray, and celebrate God. Death, in contrast, is a silence where the voice is extinguished. This underscores the importance of seeking God today, while we still have a voice, and using our lives to glorify Him before the final silence comes.

sens: Son of Ishmael and ancestor of a tribe of Arabia
City of Judah near Hebron
Prophetic name for Edom evoking silence and death
H1746G.detail:
1. Duma is primarily a man, the son of Ishmael, mentioned in Genesis 25:14 and 1 Chronicles 1:30 among the twelve sons of Ishmael. He is likely the founder of a tribe of Arabs that bore his name in antiquity.
2. The same name also designates a city located in the mountainous region of Judah, not far from Hebron, mentioned alongside other localities in the territory of Judah.
3. In prophecies (notably Isaiah 21:11), Duma becomes a mystical name for Edom, symbolizing the silence, death, and ruin that await this enemy people of Israel.
H1746G.origine: The Hebrew name דּוּמָה (duma) literally means "silence." It comes from the root דּוּם (dum), which evokes silence or immobility. This etymology is particularly meaningful for the land of Edom in the prophetic oracles, where the silence of Duma contrasts with the cry of the watchmen.
H1746G.emploi: Duma appears twice in the biblical genealogies: in Genesis 25:14 and 1 Chronicles 1:30, both listing the sons of Ishmael. These lists establish the ancestors of the pre-Islamic Arab peoples. The genealogical context shows that Duma, like his brothers Kedar, Tema, and Nebaioth, is a founding ancestor of a nomadic tribe in the Arabian desert. Beyond these historical passages, the name takes on a symbolic prophetic dimension in the oracles against Edom.
H1746G.portee: For the Christian reader, Duma embodies the origins of the Arab peoples in God's plan and reminds us that all nations descend from a common ancestor. The prophetic name of Duma applied to Edom teaches that God's judgment brings silence and death to those who persist in hostility toward His people—a lesson in the fear of the Lord.

sens: Region of Edom symbolizing the silence of death
H1746H.detail: 1. Duma is a poetic name for Edom, the kingdom in the southeast of Canaan. In the prophetic poem of Isaiah 21:11, this name evokes "silence"—not a happy peace, but the absence of life, the mutism of one who has nothing left to say, annihilated. The oracle addresses Duma and asks what it can say of the night: it is an ironic invitation to a land doomed to ruin and eternal silence.
H1746H.origine: The name Duma means "silence" in Hebrew, from the root dum which means "to be mute" or "to keep silent." It is a mystical nickname chosen by the prophet to paint the state of Edom after its judgment: the silence of death, the impossibility of speaking. The word evokes the idea of an extinguished life, a voice that no longer exists.
H1746H.emploi: Duma appears only once in the Bible, in Isaiah 21:11, in a prophetic oracle against Edom. This verse is part of a series of judgments against the nations. The prophet addresses Duma (Edom) by asking the watchman what it observes of the night—an image of impending judgment. The chosen name emphasizes that this once-powerful land will be reduced to silence by the hand of God.
H1746H.portee: This name reminds us that God's word will be fulfilled against all who oppose Him. The final silence that Edom suffers invites the reader to seriously consider God's warnings: there comes a moment when it is too late to plead one's case.

sens: Absence of noise, of speech
State of tranquility and rest
Peaceful waiting, trust in God
H1747.detail:
1. Silence is the absence of sound and speech: it is to remain mute, to say nothing. In Psalm 39:3, the psalmist remains "in silence"—he is silent, even though his heart suffers and boils internally.
2. Silence also denotes a state of rest and calm, far from tumult and agitation. In Psalm 22:3, the faithful cries out to God day and night without receiving an apparent answer, and he lacks the rest that would reassure him.
3. Finally, the word evokes confident, peaceful waiting: it is to stand still, to rely on God without agitation. In Psalm 65:2, we praise God "with confidence" (literally "in silence," that is, in peace and surrender to His word)—an attitude of listening and faith.
H1747.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to be mute, silent." It is related to the idea of remaining still and tranquil, of not making noise. The family of the word includes the adjective that describes what is silent. The basic image is that of someone who closes their mouth and remains at peace.
H1747.emploi: This word appears four times in the Psalms, at the most intense moments of prayer. In Psalm 22:3, the psalmist declares that he is deprived of rest despite his cries. In Psalm 39:3, he chooses silence to endure his pain. In Psalm 62:2 (not shown but referenced), the idea of peaceful silence returns. In Psalm 65:2, silence takes on the meaning of trust and waiting: it is the posture of one who praises God while relying on Him. The word thus shifts from the physical sense (not speaking) to the spiritual sense (trusting in silence).
H1747.portee: This word invites the reader to rediscover that silence is not the absence of faith, but sometimes its deepest expression. When God seems not to respond, silence becomes waiting and trust. It is a lesson against sterile agitation: learning to remain still, to listen, and to praise God even when everything seems empty.

sens: The absence of noise, the state of one who does not speak or shout
The attitude of one who accepts without complaint what happens to them
The inability to communicate, to speak
H1748.detail: 1. Silence is primarily the absence of sound or speech. This is what the Chaldeans experience when they are commanded: "Sit in silence, and go into darkness" (Isaiah 47:5) — they must cease to dominate, to shout, to claim. 2. Silence can also be a virtue: it is waiting patiently without revolt, as expressed in Lamentations 3:26: "It is good to wait quietly for the salvation of the Lord." It is the trust that holds back complaint. 3. Silence also characterizes that which has no life or voice: a "dumb" stone (Habakkuk 2:19) cannot speak or give counsel, even if covered in gold — it is dead, without spirit.
H1748.origine: The Hebrew word דּוּמָם comes from a root meaning "to be still, without voice." It is close to the verb "dûm" (to remain silent, to be quiet). It is a concrete word: silence as the absence of noise, then as the attitude of one who accepts, who does not defend themselves.
H1748.emploi: The word appears only three times in the Hebrew Bible. It first describes the silence imposed on a defeated people (Isaiah 47:5). It then describes the chosen silence of the believer who trusts God while waiting for His help (Lamentations 3:26) — it is a context of faith and patience amid suffering. Finally, it characterizes the mute incapacity of false gods (Habakkuk 2:19) — the silence of lies and death, since an idol can neither speak nor act.
H1748.portee: This word teaches the reader a double lesson. First, silence can be imposed by defeat or oppression. But above all, waiting in silence is a mark of faith: it is renouncing one's cries and complaints to submit to God. This trusting silence — very different from forced silence — becomes a Christian virtue, a form of listening and patience.

sens: Pale, solid, and flammable substance that melts with heat
Hardness or firmness that flows and disappears
God's power that melts all resistance
H1749.detail:
1. Wax is a solid and opaque material, known for melting quickly when heated. This is the primary meaning of the word in biblical texts.
2. When wax melts, it evokes the image of something firm losing its solidity and flowing away — which is why the psalmists use it to describe a heart that melts with anguish ("My heart is like wax; it melts within me" in Psalms 22:15) or bones that separate.
3. Furthermore, melting wax becomes the quintessential biblical image of the destruction of the wicked and God's power against opposing forces. Mountains, symbols of solidity, melt like wax before the Lord (Psalms 97:5 and Micah 1:4), while God's enemies scatter "like wax melts in the fire" (Psalms 68:3).
H1749.origine: The Hebrew word דּוּמָם refers to wax, probably from bees, well known in the ancient East as a valuable product for lighting and rituals. Its image of melting under heat makes it a natural comparison in biblical poetry, as it illustrates the rapid and complete disappearance of what seemed solid.
H1749.emploi: The word appears 4 times in the Hebrew Bible, always in Psalms or Prophets, and always in a context of comparison ("like wax"). It is never used to speak of wax in the literal sense — there is no mention of wax objects or manufacturing — but always figuratively to express melting, dissolution. In the laments (Psalms 22), it illustrates the physical and moral weakness of the suffering righteous. In hymns of divine judgment (Psalms 68, 97 and Micah 1), it depicts the destruction of the wicked and the manifestation of God's sovereignty before which nothing can resist.
H1749.portee: The melting wax teaches the believer that no earthly power, however formidable, can stand before the presence of God. It also comforts those who suffer by showing that their weakness is not shameful: even mountains melt. Finally, it reminds us that true solidity does not come from apparent strength, but from trust in the One whose power transforms everything.

sens: To leap into the air with force and speed
To jump with a quick and sudden movement
Figuratively: to suddenly emerge, to manifest with vigor
H1750.detail:
1. To leap means to jump or spring up vigorously from the ground, like an animal taking off. In Job 41:13, terror "leaps" before the Leviathan: it is the image of fear that bursts forth, that violently emerges at the sight of this terrifying creature.
2. The word describes a rapid and lively movement, that of a creature that rises abruptly. It is the leap of a beast that moves with power.
3. Used figuratively, to leap expresses the suddenness and force with which something appears or seizes us: terror leaps, it does not come gently, it bursts forth violently.
H1750.origine: The verb דּוּם evokes the image of a vigorous jump, a bodily thrust upward. It belongs to the vocabulary of lively and energetic bodily movements, very concrete in Semitic languages, where verbs often describe precise actions of the body.
H1750.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Bible, in Job 41:13, where it describes the terror leaping before the Leviathan. It is a rare verb that emphasizes, through its force and liveliness, the impression of horror that this mythical creature provokes. The epic context of the Leviathan gives this verb a grand and terrifying significance.
H1750.portee: This word reminds us that fear can seize us suddenly, with force, like something that emerges within us without warning. In the face of God's mysteries and creatures that escape our understanding, we discover how powerful and immediate terror can be.

sens: To reside, to dwell in a place
To accumulate, to pile up materials or objects
H1752.detail:
1. To dwell means to live in a place, to fix one's residence there. In Psalm 84:11, the psalmist states that he prefers to "dwell" at the threshold of God's house (that is, to serve humbly there) rather than to live comfortably in the tents of the wicked: the verb describes the act of residing somewhere, of making one's life in a place.
2. To pile up means to accumulate, to stack things on top of each other. In Ezekiel 24:5, God commands: "pile up wood under the cauldron" — it is about gathering and stacking wood to fuel the fire. The word expresses the action of bringing together materials and layering them.
H1752.origine: The Hebrew verb דּוּם comes from a root that evokes the idea of gathering, forming a group or a pile. The primary meaning is "to pile up" or "to accumulate"; the meaning of "to dwell" naturally follows: to inhabit somewhere is to "remain assembled" in a place, to make one's home there. Aramaic uses the same word (דּוּם) with the meaning of "to dwell." This root is connected to the idea of concentration and stability in space.
H1752.emploi: This very rare verb in biblical Hebrew appears only twice in the Old Testament. In Psalms 84:11, it describes the psalmist's desire to reside with God, expressing a deep spiritual aspiration: to prefer one day of closeness to God over a thousand days far from Him. In Ezekiel 24:5, the same verb (in the imperative form) refers to the accumulation of wood as a concrete material. These two uses show that דּוּם oscillates between a spiritual meaning (residence, dwelling) and a material meaning (piling up). The context determines which of the two meanings predominates.
H1752.portee: For the believer reading Psalm 84:11, this word invites reflection on what they truly desire: to dwell with God is to seek His presence and communion above all earthly prosperity. This aspiration to "remain" with God reveals that true life is found in closeness to Him, not in the abundance of the world. It is a call to faithfulness and to prioritize God in our lives.

sens: To dwell, reside in a place
To occupy a space, to settle there
To find refuge, to shelter somewhere
H1753.detail:
1. To dwell means to reside, to have a fixed home in a place. When King Nebuchadnezzar writes "to all peoples, nations, and men of every language, who dwell on all the earth" (Daniel 4:1), he refers to the populations that live, that are settled on the earth. It is the idea of making one's home somewhere, of having one's usual seat there.
2. To dwell can also simply express the occupation of a space or condition: in Daniel 2:38, God has given into the hands of the king "wherever they dwell" the children of men — in other words, wherever they are, wherever they live. The meaning is that of occupying, of being situated in.
3. In a figurative sense, to dwell takes on the meaning of taking shelter, finding refuge: in Daniel 4:12, "the beasts of the field took shelter under the shade" of the tree, and "the birds of the sky made their dwelling among its branches." Here, to dwell means to find a place of protection, of rest.
H1753.origine: This Aramaic word dur comes from the same root as the Hebrew verb dûr (דּוּר, H1752), which carries the same meaning of "to dwell, to reside." It is a very ancient verb, expressing the natural and elemental idea of fixing one's habitation somewhere. The root evokes the act of establishing oneself, of making a circle around a home or territory.
H1753.emploi: The verb to dwell appears six times in the book of Daniel, a text written in Aramaic (like this word). It is used to describe where creatures, peoples, or living beings live: men (Daniel 2:38, 4:1, 6:25), the beasts and the birds that take refuge in a tree (Daniel 4:12, 4:21), or all of humanity under God's reign (Daniel 4:35). The context of the usages suggests that the word carries a cosmic and theological significance: it is less about describing a domestic dwelling than about expressing where each has its place in the created world, under God's sovereign control and the king He establishes.
H1753.portee: This word invites the reader to reflect on their place in the created world. To dwell is to recognize that one does not possess the earth absolutely, but lives there by God's permission and governance. The repetition of this verb in the royal proclamations of Daniel emphasizes that every inhabitant, from the most powerful king to the humblest people, dwells under divine authority and has their life and rest only through His maintenance.

sens: round shape, closed circuit
fortified structure surrounding a city
group of people or things arranged in a circle
H1754A.detail:
1. The primary meaning is that of a round, closed shape, like a drawn circle or a spherical object: it is the simple idea of something that has no beginning or end, which constantly returns upon itself.
2. In a military or urban context, the word refers to the enclosures or fortifications that surround a city to protect it or besiege it. Isaiah 29:3 speaks of God who "will camp against you in a circle," forming a line of encirclement around Jerusalem like an army besieging it.
3. By extension, it can refer to any group of people or things arranged in a circular formation around a center.
H1754A.origine: The Hebrew word דּוּר comes from a root that evokes the idea of turning or curling. The basic image is that of circular movement, of perpetual return, from which the meanings of "circle" or "enclosure" derive. It is a rather rare word in the Bible, but carries a powerful and concrete image.
H1754A.emploi: The word appears only once in the provided biblical texts, in Isaiah 29:3, where it describes God's action of encircling Jerusalem during a siege. This military context highlights the aspect of encirclement and limitation of space. Although rare, the word plays an important role in this prophetic passage, where the very shape of the circle evokes the relentlessness of divine judgment.
H1754A.portee: This word reminds us that God's encirclement of Jerusalem is not an arbitrary or temporary act, but a judgment that progressively closes the perimeter of His action. For the reader, the image of the tightening circle invites meditation on the reality of divine judgment and the impossibility of escaping it when opposing God. It is also an image of totality and exhaustiveness: nothing remains outside the circle of judgment.

sens: spherical or rounded object that can roll
round, circular shape
cord wound, thing tied in a circle
H1754B.detail:
1. A ball is a round object that can roll or be thrown — this is the most common and concrete meaning of the word. In Isaiah 22:18, the prophet uses this image to describe God's judgment: the unworthy king will be rolled like a ball on a spacious land, expelled uncontrollably, tumultuously, until his death.
2. The word can simply refer to a round or circular shape, the spherical aspect of an object.
3. By extension, it can refer to a cord or band wound in a circle, a thing tied in a round — a less common image but attested in the Hebrew lexical tradition.
H1754B.origine: The Hebrew word כַּדּוּר (kad.dur) likely comes from a root expressing the idea of circulating, turning, or rolling. The form recalls Hebrew words denoting circle and rotation. It is a simple and concrete word, born from the observation of round objects in daily life.
H1754B.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 22:18. The prophet Isaiah uses it in an oracle against a high official of the king of Judah who abuses his power. The image of the rolled ball evokes humiliation and rapid expulsion, without dignity — a metaphor for divine judgment that drives the guilty far from their honor and power.
H1754B.portee: This image invites meditation on God's judgment against those who abuse the entrusted power. The uncontrollable rolled ball reminds us that no human power can resist when God pronounces His judgment: man must recognize that his strength is nothing and that only divine justice prevails.

sens: Group of people born and living at the same time
All direct descendants of a person or lineage
Duration of a human life or a historical period
Distinctive character of people of the same time
Dwelling, habitat
H1755.detail: 1. A generation primarily refers to the group of people who live together at the same time: it is the "time" in which they exist. When Noah walked with God "in his generation" (Genesis 6:9), it refers to his generation, the people of his time, and his own life. 2. The word also designates direct descendants, the continuation of those who are born and perpetuate a lineage. When God tells Abraham that his descendants will observe the Sabbath "among your descendants" (Exodus 31:13), He is speaking of those who will be born from him. 3. A generation can also mark a measurable period of time: "in the times to come" (Numbers 15:21) for future generations who will fulfill the law. 4. The word often characterizes the moral quality of an era: a "perverse generation" (Deuteronomy 32:5) or a "generation" that believes itself pure (Proverbs 30:12) describes the people of the time, with their flaws. 5. Rarely, the word can mean "dwelling" or "habitat," as a generation also exists within a given place of life.
H1755.origine: The Hebrew word dor comes from a root meaning to turn, to go around, which evokes the continuous cycle of life: generations succeed one another like the seasons. In Hebrew, it appears in expressions about duration and eternity: "from generation to generation" (Esther 9:28) shows how this word marks the continuity of time. The word can also evoke habitat or dwelling, as a generation "inhabits" a given time, a place, an era.
H1755.emploi: This word appears 127 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the Pentateuch (the books of Moses), the Psalms, and Esther. It most often designates a generation of people living at the same time: the generations that will see the wonders of God (Psalms 22:31, 79:13), or who will violate His commandments (Deuteronomy 32:5, 32:20). The word also serves to mark ritual and legal continuity: the laws that each generation must observe "forever" (Exodus 12:14, Exodus 31:13). Finally, it can designate a limited duration of time: "there are forty years" expresses an entire generation (Numbers 32:13, Deuteronomy 2:14), the time that a generation goes through before disappearing.
H1755.portee: This word reminds the reader that each generation has its own responsibility before God: it must know His works and commandments, and it must pass them on to those who will come after (Psalms 71:18). It emphasizes the importance of passing on faith from generation to generation, so that the memory of divine wonders never fades. It is a call to spiritual continuity over time.

sens: coastal city of Palestine, south of Carmel
possession of the tribe of Manasseh
site of resistance to the Israelite conquest
H1756G.detail: 1. Dor is a coastal city located south of Carmel, in the land of Canaan. It was situated near the Mediterranean Sea and formed an important urban center in the region. 2. The tribe of Manasseh received Dor as an inheritance during the division of the promised land (Joshua 17:11 and 1 Chronicles 7:29), along with its surrounding villages, although the city was initially governed by a Canaanite king (Joshua 12:23). 3. The Canaanites resided in Dor and refused to leave despite the arrival of the Israelites: Manasseh did not drive out the inhabitants of Dor (Judges 1:27), which shows that the conquest there was incomplete and that the Canaanite population persisted for a long time.
H1756G.origine: The Hebrew name dor literally means "generation" or "habitation"; it designates here a city whose Hebrew identity likely comes from this archaic sense of "dwelling." The archaeological site of Dor, identified with khirbet el-Burj near Nablus, bears witness to continuous human presence from ancient Near Eastern times to the classical period.
H1756G.emploi: Dor appears four times in the Hebrew Bible: in Joshua 12:23 among the cities of the kings defeated by Joshua, in Joshua 17:11 and 1 Chronicles 7:29 as a possession assigned to Manasseh, and in Judges 1:27 as an example of a city whose Canaanite inhabitants were not expelled. These usages show that Dor gradually came under Israelite control but was never fully conquered during the time of the Judges.
H1756G.portee: Dor illustrates the incompleteness of the conquest: although the promised land was given to Israel, some cities remained in the hands of the Canaanites, reminding us that obedience to God was not perfect from the beginning. It is a lesson on the consequences of half-victory and the necessity of total commitment in God's work.

sens: coastal city of the territory of Manasseh, in Canaan
region or territory administered including this city
H1756H.detail: 1. Dor is a coastal city located in northern Canaan, in the territory of Manasseh, south of Carmel (Joshua 11:2). It had a strategic position near the Mediterranean, as indicated by the expressions "on the heights of Dor" and "Dor to the west." 2. The name Dor also designates the region or territory that depended on this city — a land administered as a unit under the authority of a king or governor, as seen when "the son of Abinadab had all the region of Dor" (1 Kings 4:11).
H1756H.origine: The Hebrew name דֹּאר (dor) comes from a root meaning "to dwell" or "to reside." Dor was one of the major coastal cities of Canaan, occupied by the Canaanites before the Israelite conquest, and its name reflects its importance as an established and fortified place. The modern site is identified with Khirbet el-Burj on the current Mediterranean coast of Israel.
H1756H.emploi: Dor appears three times in the Bible. During the conquest of Canaan, Joshua confronts the king of Dor among the Canaanite kings (Joshua 11:2 and 12:23), which shows that it was a major stronghold. After the conquest, during the reign of King Solomon, Dor becomes the seat of an administrative district governed by the son of Abinadab, who must provide for the king's sustenance (1 Kings 4:11). The city thus transitions from the status of a Canaanite royal capital to that of an Israelite administrative center.

sens: Place in Babylon where King Nebuchadnezzar set up a golden statue
H1757.detail: Dura is a valley or plain located in Babylon, in the empire of King Nebuchadnezzar. It is in this place that the king erected the famous golden statue of sixty cubits in height, before which he commanded all the peoples of his empire to bow down (Daniel 3:1). The exact site of this Dura is uncertain, but the biblical context indicates that it was an important and accessible location, capable of hosting a massive assembly of dignitaries from all provinces.
H1757.origine: The word literally means "dwelling" or "place of habitation" in Aramaic. It comes from a root that evokes the idea of dwelling or residing. Its use to designate this Babylonian valley reflects the importance of the place as an established and recognized location within the empire.
H1757.emploi: The word Dura appears only once in the Bible, in Daniel 3:1, where it specifically designates the valley where Nebuchadnezzar erected the golden statue. This context is crucial: it is the setting for the narrative where three young Hebrews — Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego — refuse to bow down before the idol and are thrown into a fiery furnace. The name of the place is not given elsewhere in the Scriptures, suggesting that it is a precise historical detail of the narrative.

sens: To walk on something, to crush it underfoot
To trample, to mistreat by walking on it
To thresh grain: to walk on it to detach the grains
To crush, to grind, to reduce to crumbs
Figuratively: to humiliate, to reduce to nothing
H1758.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to walk on something or someone with force: to place one's foot to crush what is on the ground. In Deuteronomy 25:4, the ox "treads the grain" by walking on it to thresh it. In 2 Kings 13:7, the enemies have "made the people like dust that is trampled underfoot," an image of complete destruction.
2. To trample means to walk heavily and repeatedly on something to damage or destroy it. It is the same verb, but it emphasizes the repeated and violent action. Job 39:18 mentions a case where "a beast of the field can trample them" — this means to walk on something with brutality.
3. To thresh grain is a specific agricultural technique: to make animals walk over the ears of grain or to pass a sled over them to detach the grains. Hosea 10:11 describes Ephraim as a "trained heifer that loves to tread grain," an image of a plowing beast accustomed to this work. Isaiah 28:27 specifies the methods: one "does not tread the cumin with a sled" but "beats it with a stick."
4. To crush and grind refer to the final effect: to reduce to fine fragments or dust. Isaiah 41:15 uses "you shall crush and grind the mountains" to express a total and overwhelming victory.
5. Figuratively, to tread means to humiliate or reduce to powerlessness. Jeremiah 50:11 says that Babylon "treads" Judah, not literally but by oppressing it. Amos 1:3 denounces the one who "treads" the Gileadites, meaning persecutes them.
H1758.origine: The verb dush (דּוּשׁ) comes from a Semitic root that evokes the action of walking heavily, of trampling. It is a very concrete verb, rooted in the daily life of the ancient Near East where threshing the harvest was an essential task. The same word appears in other contexts to express any form of crushing, from grain to enemies.
H1758.emploi: This verb appears 14 times in the Old Testament, mainly in texts related to agriculture (Deuteronomy, Isaiah, Hosea) and battles (Amos, Micah, Habakkuk). Its agricultural use is literal: to thresh grain by animals or a sled. But as early as ancient Assyria, the verb extends to the warrior and political domain: to "tread" an enemy or a people means to conquer, humiliate, reduce to powerlessness. Isaiah 41:15 uses the image of threshing the harvest to describe the overwhelming victory of God's servant. In Jeremiah 50:11 and Amos 1:3, it is an act of cruelty: to tread a people means to persecute them mercilessly. The context indicates whether the word is literal or figurative.
H1758.portee: This verb reminds us that God does not tolerate the crushing of the weak or treating them like grain to be threshed. In Deuteronomy 25:4, the law even protects the ox that treads the grain: it is a lesson in justice. Conversely, Isaiah 41:15 assures that God will make the people an instrument to break the oppressors. The word confronts us with the real violence of the world and the promise that God will judge those who unjustly crush others.

sens: To walk or trample on something with force, to subdue it by violence
H1759.detail: 1. To tread means to walk on something brutally to crush or dominate it. It is the action of trampling. In Daniel 7:23, the fourth beast "will tread" the whole earth: the image is of a beast that crushes everything under its feet, symbolizing a kingdom that crushes peoples and exercises total and destructive domination over them.
H1759.origine: The Aramaic word דּוּשׁ (dush) comes from the same root as the Hebrew דּוּשׁ (dush, H1758) which means "to tread" or "to crush." This root evokes the physical action of walking heavily on something to destroy it. In Hebrew, this verb is used to describe the action of treading grapes during harvest, or trampling an adversary.
H1759.emploi: This Aramaic verb appears only once in the New Testament (according to the provided definition) and once in the reported biblical text. It is found in Daniel 7:23, in the prophetic vision of the prophet Daniel. The fourth beast is seen treading the whole earth, meaning to subdue and completely crush it. The context is that of the visions of the four successive kingdoms, and this action symbolizes the devastating and tyrannical nature of the final power before divine judgment.
H1759.portee: This word reminds the believer that brutal domination and the crushing of peoples characterize the carnal kingdoms that are hostile to God. The Bible thus teaches that earthly power, when it rejects God, becomes an instrument of oppression. For the disciple, it is an invitation not to seek security in the kingdoms of this world, but to place hope in Christ, whose reign is founded on justice and mercy, not on violence.

sens: To push someone or something violently
To make fall, to knock down
To chase away, to expel
To be thrown to the ground, to collapse
H1760A.detail:
1. The most direct meaning: to push someone with force to destabilize them. It is a violent and deliberate act. The psalmist prays: "You pushed me to make me fall" (Psalms 118:13), describing how his enemies physically press him to make him fall.
2. To make someone fall or to bring them down — not just to push, but to completely knock them down. "The wicked is overthrown by his wickedness" (Proverbs 14:32): the weight of his own actions throws him to the ground, irreparably.
3. To chase away, to expel, to put outside: "Let the angel of the Lord chase them away!" (Psalms 35:5). The word here describes a movement that distances, that banishes.
4. To undergo this action, to be thrown down or toppled: "They are overthrown, and they cannot rise" (Psalms 36:13). This is the state of one who has been struck and lies powerless.
H1760A.origine: The Hebrew verb דָּחָה (dachah) comes from a root expressing the idea of a violent push. It is related to words describing abrupt movement and forced displacement. The image is that of a body staggering or falling under the impact of an external force. This root appears mainly in the Psalms and Wisdom literature, where it expresses the hostile action of enemies or the judgment of God.
H1760A.emploi: The verb dachah appears six times in the Hebrew Bible, concentrated in the Psalms and one passage from Proverbs. In the Psalms, it is the cry of the righteous threatened: he asks God to chase away his enemies (35:5) or recalls how he was pushed to make him fall (118:13, 140:5). The context is always that of persecution and struggle. In Proverbs 14:32, the meaning broadens: wickedness itself overthrows the wicked, without the need for a human hand. The word thus expresses both the hostile action of others and the inevitable judgment that sin provokes.
H1760A.portee: This word reminds the reader that God sees the violence of the wicked and that no enemy can "overthrow" us beyond divine will. For those who suffer persecution, it affirms that divine justice will ultimately overturn the violent. It is also a call not to rely on evil, for it is sin itself that ruins us. The righteous, on the other hand, finds in God an unshakeable help.

sens: To be overturned, fallen by a force that pushes
To be routed, to be driven off one's path
H1760B.detail:
1. The verb literally describes the action of being pushed, that is, being repelled or overturned by an external force: the person loses footing and falls. In Jeremiah 23:12, the false prophets are described as having a path that becomes "slippery and dark," and they will be "pushed" — the image is that of an inevitable, forced fall.
2. Figuratively, to be "pushed" means to be routed, driven off one's path, to be defeated. This is what happens to the false prophets: not only is their path a failure, but they are actively overturned by God's judgment which "pushes" them into ruin.
H1760B.origine: This verb comes from the root דָּחָה (da.chah), which expresses the idea of repelling, pushing, driving away. The form here (Niphal) is the passive or reflexive form: it does not say "X pushes," but "X is pushed" or "X is made to be pushed." It is the opposite image of the active verb: instead of being the one who pushes, one is the one who undergoes the push.
H1760B.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Bible, in Jeremiah 23:12. It is part of a judgment pronounced against the false prophets: their path will become slippery, dark, and they will be "pushed" and fall. The context of ruin and divine punishment shows that "to be pushed" is not a passing accident, but the certain consequence of their lies.
H1760B.portee: This word reminds us that God's judgment is not a vague threat: it is a real and irresistible action that overturns those who stray from the truth. For the Christian reader, it invites examination of whether one's own path is founded on God's truth, for fear of "slipping" oneself.

sens: abstention from food and drink
voluntary renunciation of a pleasure or distraction
H1761.detail: 1. Fasting is primarily the abstention from food and drink for a certain period of time. Literally, this is what King Darius refuses to do in Daniel 6:18: he cannot deprive himself of eating or drinking, as he is tormented by worry about Daniel thrown into the lions' den. 2. More broadly, fasting extends to any form of voluntary renunciation of what pleases or comforts. When Daniel 6:18 says that the king "did not bring a concubine to him," it shows that fasting can mean renouncing a pleasure or distraction, as a mark of concern or mourning.
H1761.origine: The Aramaic word דַּחֲוָה comes from the verb דָּחָה ("to remove," "to push away," "to deprive"). The underlying idea is one of deprivation or renunciation: one pushes away food, pleasures, to focus on something more important. It is a word of Aramaic origin, the language spoken in the Persian empire at the time of Daniel.
H1761.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Daniel 6:18. King Darius, upset by Daniel's capture, can neither eat nor drink, nor distract himself with the pleasures of the palace: he is too preoccupied. The fasting here is not a voluntary religious act, but a reflection of the king's agitation and worry. This unique usage shows that fasting, in biblical thought, is linked to an intense inner state: mourning, fear, or spiritual fervor.
H1761.portee: This passage reminds us that fasting is not merely a superficial religious gesture, but manifests a state of the heart. When one is truly concerned about a justice to defend or a communion with God to seek, the body itself bears the mark: one forgets ordinary pleasures, renounces distractions. It is a lesson in spiritual authenticity for the Christian reader.

sens: action of falling
state of one who falls or collapses
trial or misfortune that causes a life to topple
H1762.detail:
1. The word primarily designates the physical act of falling, losing balance, and collapsing to the ground. It is a loss of stability and control of the body.
2. It extends to the idea of a collapse, a debacle: it is the condition of one who has lost footing and finds themselves in misfortune or trial.
3. In the Psalms, this word images moral or spiritual instability — the risk of sinking into distress. The psalmist prays for God to keep his feet "from falling" (Psalms 56:14), that is, to preserve him from collapse and ruin.
H1762.origine: The Hebrew word דְּחִי comes from a root meaning "to fall" or "to collapse." This image of the body losing footing expresses, in biblical thought, a tipping point that is both physical and spiritual: to fall in the literal sense is also to risk being unable to serve God or live in His light.
H1762.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Bible, both in the Psalms. In these two occurrences (Psalms 56:14 and 116:8), the psalmist gives thanks to God who has "delivered his feet from falling" — a poetic way of saying that God has saved him from misfortune and ruin. It is an image of divine protection against trials that threaten to bring us down.
H1762.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader that life involves risks and instabilities — moments when one risks collapsing. But it emphasizes the protection that God offers: He does not let us fall. To pray for preservation from falling is to acknowledge our fragility and dependence on God.

sens: To experience fear, fright in front of something or someone
To be seized with fear, anxiety
To have an aspect or appearance that inspires fear
To inspire fear, terror (causative sense)
H1763.detail:
1. To experience fear in the face of someone or something: it is the feeling provoked by what is threatening or impressive. Nebuchadnezzar in Daniel 4:5 is "afraid" of his dreams; the king in Daniel 6:26 orders that there be "fear" for the God of Daniel, meaning that He should be respected and feared as a formidable power.
2. To be overwhelmed by fear or anxiety: it is a disposition of the heart and mind in the face of what seems dangerous. The peoples in Daniel 5:19 are in "fear" and tremble before the king, expressing both the fear and respect he inspires.
3. To have an appearance or nature that provokes terror: it is when something naturally inspires fear by what it is. The statue in Daniel 2:31 is "terrible" in appearance, and the beast in Daniel 7:7 is "terrible" and "frightful," so impressive that one can only fear it.
H1763.origine: The word belongs to the family of verbs expressing fear in biblical Aramaic. It fundamentally evokes the feeling of fright and mixed respect: when one fears someone, one acknowledges their power and reacts with fear. It is a word that circulates in the accounts of the kings of Babylon and expresses absolute authority and impressive domination.
H1763.emploi: This word appears six times in Aramaic in the book of Daniel, always in the context of royal power, prophetic visions, or reverence towards God. It translates sometimes the emotion of fear (Nebuchadnezzar afraid of his dreams, Daniel 4:5), sometimes respect and submission in the face of authority (fear before the king, Daniel 5:19 and 6:26), sometimes a quality that inspires terror (the statue or the prophetic beast, Daniel 2:31, 7:7, 7:19). The word appears only in biblical Aramaic, never in classical Hebrew, which situates it in the later texts of revelations and foreign governance.
H1763.portee: For the believer, this word poses a central question: how to react in the face of what is greater, stronger than oneself? Fear can be servile and destructive, or it can be the respectful acceptance of divine power. In reading that God commands that one has fear of the living God (Daniel 6:26), we discover that authentic fear is not paralyzing dread, but a recognition of sovereignty and trust in the One who endures forever.

sens: Cereal with very fine grains, cultivated for human and animal consumption
Staple food in arid regions or during shortages
H1764.detail:
1. Millet is a productive cereal that grows easily in dry or poor regions. Its very small grains cook quickly and serve as a nourishing staple food, alongside wheat and barley. Ezekiel 4:9 mentions it among the ingredients of the survival bread that the prophet must prepare.
2. This grain primarily appears as a substitute or necessity food: when wheat is lacking or famine threatens, millet is used to survive. In the symbolic context of Ezekiel's passage, it is a humble grain that signifies the poverty and restrictions imposed on the people under judgment.
H1764.origine: The Hebrew word דֹּחַן likely comes from a root that evokes crumbling or scattering, as millet consists of tiny grains that easily detach. It is a food known in Mesopotamia and the ancient East, cultivated for millennia in hot and dry regions.
H1764.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Ezekiel 4:9. The prophet is instructed to prepare a bread mixing several humble and inexpensive grains—wheat, barley, beans, lentils, millet, and spelt—to symbolically signify the restrictions and famine that will strike besieged Jerusalem. Here, millet is not depicted as a prestigious food, but as one of the grains of scarcity, mixed with others to form a bread of misery.
H1764.portee: This humble grain reminds us that God, in judgment, can reduce abundance to strict necessity. It also symbolizes humility and dependence: even in deprivation, God provides for the survival of His people. It is a call to recognize that all that nourishes comes from His hand, whether in wealth or poverty.

sens: To act or depart with speed, without delay
To hurry, to accomplish something quickly
To accelerate movement, to go fast
H1765.detail:
1. The word describes the action of moving or acting without delay, with urgency. It means to move or leave quickly due to a circumstance that compels one not to linger. When King Azariah sees leprosy on King Uzziah's forehead, the priests "hurry" him out quickly (2 Chronicles 26:20): they act fast, pressed by the horror of the situation.
2. The word is also used to express the urgency of a departure or message. The king's couriers leave "in all haste" to spread the edict throughout the empire (Esther 3:15 and 8:14): they hurry, riding quickly, because the royal order demands speed and efficiency.
3. Sometimes it simply means to act with eagerness or diligence. When Haman "hurries" to return home after losing favor with the king (Esther 6:12), it is because he is fleeing quickly, without waiting, driven by fear and shame.
H1765.origine: The Hebrew word דָּחַף (da.chaph) comes from a root that conveys the idea of pushing or chasing quickly. It is related to other Hebrew words expressing urgency and rapid movement. The image of departure is that of a force pushing forward: one pushes something or someone to move quickly, without allowing time to linger or resist.
H1765.emploi: This word appears 4 times in the Hebrew Bible, always with the nuance of speed and urgency. It is mainly found in late historical narratives (2 Chronicles and Esther), in contexts where action must be immediate. In 2 Chronicles 26:20, it is the king who is hurried out of the temple. In the three passages from the book of Esther (3:15, 6:12, 8:14), it qualifies urgent departures: either the couriers executing the king's order in haste, or Haman fleeing in shame. Each time, the context reinforces the idea that delay cannot be tolerated.
H1765.portee: This word reminds us that there are moments when obedience and action cannot tolerate delay. For the Christian reader, it awakens the awareness of the urgent nature of certain decisions or calls: not to linger, not to hesitate when God or an authority demands action. It is also an invitation to reflect on what truly justifies urgency in life.

sens: To exert physical pressure on something or someone, to squeeze or push
To overwhelm someone under the weight of domination or suffering
To cause distress or anguish to someone
H1766.detail:
1. The primary meaning is physical: it is to push, press, or squeeze with force. In Joel 2:8, the locusts do not press against one another as they advance—they keep their ranks tight without jostling, united in their march.
2. The word then takes on a more serious meaning: to oppress means to subject someone to overwhelming authority, to exploit or mistreat them. In Judges 2:18, the enemies "oppressed" the people of Israel, tormenting and crushing them, until God sent them a deliverer.
3. More broadly, to oppress is to cause distress, to weigh heavily on someone's heart and mind—hence the idea of anguish and groaning in those who suffer this oppression.
H1766.origine: The Hebrew root דָּחַק expresses primarily a physical action of pressure or compression. It evokes the image of squeezing, pressing against oneself, or pushing. The word belongs to a semantic family where the idea of force and constraint is central: it is always an action that imposes a limit or suffering on the one who endures it.
H1766.emploi: The verb דָּחַק appears twice in the provided biblical usages. First in the concrete sense in Joel 2:8, where it describes the locusts advancing in tight formation. Then in the social and spiritual sense in Judges 2:18, where it qualifies the oppression that the enemies inflict on Israel—a weight of domination and torment from which only God can deliver His people. The meaning naturally shifts from physical pressure to domination and moral distress.
H1766.portee: This word reminds the reader of the reality of suffering and oppression in this world, and even more so of God's heart towards those who groan under the weight. In Judges 2:18, it shows that God "hears" the cries of His oppressed people and sends them deliverers: it is a promise that our distress is never ignored by Him.

sens: What is enough, what meets a given need
The appropriate number or quantity for a situation
Each time, as often as
According to the measure of, proportionately to
H1767.detail:
1. Sufficiency is what is enough to accomplish a task: in Exodus 36:5, the people bring "much more than enough" to build the sanctuary — the word here denotes the necessary and sufficient quantity.
2. It is also the right number, suitable for each case: in Deuteronomy 25:2, the judge strikes the guilty party with "a number of blows proportionate to the severity of his fault" — neither too many nor too few.
3. The word also expresses regular repetition: in Isaiah 66:23, "at each new moon" means "each time the moon is new" — it is a frequency that recurs according to an established rhythm.
4. Finally, it marks a limit or a suitable measure: in Proverbs 25:16, "eat only what is sufficient for you" invites respect for the proper portion so that good does not turn into evil.
H1767.origine: The Hebrew word דַּי (day) comes from a root that fundamentally means "to be enough" or "to suffice." It expresses the idea of a natural or suitable limit — what exceeds or what is lacking does not fall under this word. It is found in other Hebrew forms that denote sufficiency and measured abundance. It is a simple and very concrete word: it speaks of what exactly fulfills its function.
H1767.emploi: This word appears 35 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in historical narratives, laws, and wisdom literature. It is used to express ideas of satisfied need (Proverbs 25:16: eating to sufficiency), regulatory quantity (Deuteronomy 25:2: the number of blows), and regular repetition (Isaiah 66:23: at each Sabbath). It can also mean "capable of" or "able to" in certain contexts (Leviticus 5:7: "if he does not have enough"). Its meaning varies depending on whether it modifies a noun (then it means "enough of," "the desired number of") or follows a verb (then it means "to suffice for"). The word is particularly frequent in ritual laws and descriptions of regular practices.
H1767.portee: This word invites the believer to recognize that God provides for our true needs and that sufficiency — not excess — is the sign of a balanced life. It also reminds us that God's rules aim for fairness and measure, not arbitrariness: a punishment must be proportionate to the fault, a sacrifice suited to the capacity of the faithful. Finally, it encourages respect for the rhythms that God has established — Sabbaths, feasts — that the believer observes "each time" with regularity.

sens: Relative pronoun introducing a relative clause: refers to a person or thing mentioned previously
Marks the relationship of belonging or possession: "the one of", "that which belongs to"
Conjunction introducing a subordinate clause of complement or purpose
Marks a causal relationship: "because", "since"
H1768.detail:
1. The word introduces a clause that describes or completes the preceding noun or noun group. For example, in Daniel 4:20, "the tree that you saw": the word connects "tree" to the description of what it has become. It is the fundamental grammatical link between a thing and the clarifications given about it.

2. It often marks possession or belonging, an idea rendered in French by "of." In Daniel 2:14, "Arjoc, chief of the king": literally, Arjoc is the chief "who belongs to" or "who depends on" the king. This relationship establishes a dependence or a relationship of subordination.
