3. As a conjunction, it introduces an idea expressed in a subordinate clause, often to indicate purpose, consequence, or the content of an action. In Daniel 6:2, "so that these satraps might give an account to them": the word introduces the result or the desired purpose.

4. It can also express a causal relationship, marking "why" or "because" something happens or is so — a more subtle nuance but present in certain Aramaic contexts.
H1768.origine: This Aramaic word is an extremely common particle in the biblical Aramaic sections of Daniel and Ezra. It functions as a universal connector, replacing or complementing several grammatical tools. Its usage reflects the needs of the Aramaic language to link elements of a sentence, somewhat like the Greek "hos" or the French "que." The particle has a common Semitic origin among the ancient Near Eastern languages.
H1768.emploi: This word is used 185 times in the Hebrew Bible, concentrated almost exclusively in the Aramaic portions: Daniel (chapter 2 in particular, with about 40 occurrences) and Ezra (where it appears massively in chapters 4 to 7). It is a fundamental grammatical particle of the Aramaic dialect of these books. It functions to introduce relative clauses ("who," "that"), mark possession ("of"), or join subordinate clauses ("that," "so that"). Its frequency reveals a language shift: these sections of the Bible transition from Hebrew to the imperial Aramaic dialect spoken at the Persian court. Almost all uses are purely grammatical, serving syntax.

sens: City of Moab east of the Jordan
Region rebuilt by the sons of Gad
Place of worship and lamentation
H1769G.detail:
1. Dibon is a Moabite city located on the eastern bank of the Jordan, strategically situated in the plain of Medeba. It appears in the conquest narratives of Israel: it was initially a city of the Moabites, then taken by Israel and rebuilt by the tribe of Gad (Numbers 32:34).

2. The city became one of the fortified cities of the Gadite territory, mentioned alongside other important posts like Ataroth and Aroer (Joshua 13:9, 13:17). It marked the northern boundary of the land of Moab after the conquest.

3. Dibon was also a Moabite religious center, with a temple where mourning rites were performed, showing its importance in the religious life of Moab (Isaiah 15:2). During the Assyrian invasions, it became a place of lamentation for the misfortunes of the Moabite people.
H1769G.origine: The name Dibon likely means "ruin" or "destruction," evoking the idea of desolation. Archaeology has identified it with present-day Dhîbân, in Jordan, where the famous Moabite Stone of King Mesha (9th century BC) was discovered, mentioning the rebuilding of Dibon and speaking of the wars between Moab and Israel.
H1769G.emploi: Dibon is mentioned 8 times in the Bible, mainly in conquest passages (Numbers and Joshua) and in oracles against Moab (Isaiah 15, Jeremiah 48). It embodies both a victory for Israel and an important center of Moabite power. Its name recurs in prophetic texts announcing the fall of Moab, highlighting its key role in regional history.

sens: city in southern Judea
place of residence for Judeans upon return from captivity
H1769H.detail: 1. Dibon is a city located in the southern region of Judea. 2. After the exile in Babylon, the men of Judah resettle there, as reported in Nehemiah (Nehemiah 11:25): it is listed among the cities where the sons of Judah establish their dwelling again in the territories that belong to them.
H1769H.origine: The name Dibon literally means "devastation" or "ruin," perhaps reflecting the state of the region after the destruction from invasions. However, the name of this city also appears in the Old Testament in reference to a city of the Moabites (mentioned in Numbers and Jeremiah), suggesting a long history of occupation and settlement in the area.
H1769H.emploi: Dibon appears only once in the Segond in the sense of a Judean place: in Nehemiah 11:25, during the enumeration of cities where the Judeans resettle after the return from captivity. The context shows that this city is part of the important centers of settlement in southern Judea during the reconstruction of the land. This mention is part of the restoration project of Israel after the Babylonian exile.
H1769H.portee: The return of Dibon to Judean life symbolizes the renewal and restoration that God grants to His people after the exile. This name reminds us that devastation is not permanent: abandoned lands are repopulated, ruined cities are reborn. It is a sign of the fulfillment of God's promises of restoration.

sens: City of Moab east of the Jordan
Territory conquered by the Israelites and rebuilt by the children of Gad
H1769I.detail: 1. Dibon-Gad is a city located in Moab, on the east bank of the Jordan, in the region that became the territory of the children of Gad after the conquest of Canaan. 2. The Israelites took possession of this city and rebuilt it; it served as a stopping point during the migrations of the people through the desert (Numbers 33:45-46).
H1769I.origine: The name literally means "waste" or "decay," perhaps referring to the arid nature of the region or its history. The full name "Dibon-Gad" associates the name of the city with that of the tribe of Gad, which rebuilt and inhabited it after the conquest.
H1769I.emploi: Dibon-Gad appears twice in the Book of Numbers, in the account of the desert stations (Numbers 33:45-46). The city is mentioned as a stop on the journey of the Israelites coming out of Egypt, between Ijjé-Abarim and Almon-Diblathaim. It illustrates the geography of the Transjordan lands that the children of Gad received as an inheritance.

sens: To catch fish with a net, line, or trap
Figuratively, to seek to capture or take someone
H1770.detail:
1. To fish literally means to catch fish in the water using nets, lines, or other equipment. It is a common profession in Israel and elsewhere in the ancient East, especially near the Sea of Galilee and the Jordan. In Jeremiah 16:16, the Lord speaks of sending "fishermen" to "fish" for the people — the image shows how fish are skillfully and intentionally captured.
2. Figuratively, to fish refers to the action of seeking to attract or capture someone, as one catches prey. In Jeremiah 16:16, God compares judgment on Israel to fishing: the fishermen and hunters represent the enemy nations that will capture and take the Israelites — a powerful image of the inevitability of divine punishment.
H1770.origine: The word comes from a simple Hebrew root that means "to catch" or "to capture by cunning." It is related to the general idea of seizing something that does not want to be taken. The verb is commonly used in biblical Hebrew for all types of capture: fish, game, or figuratively, people.
H1770.emploi: The verb "to fish" appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Jeremiah 16:16. In this judgment passage, God first sends "fishermen" to capture the Israelites hiding in the lands, then "hunters" to pursue them in the mountains and rocks. The use of the verb to fish here is entirely metaphorical: it emphasizes how the people, fleeing divine judgment, will be captured as inevitably as a fish cannot escape the fisherman's net.
H1770.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader that nothing can escape God's judgment when it comes — no more than a fish can flee forever in the waters. It also speaks, conversely, of God's call: Jesus calls his disciples to become "fishers of men," that is, to seek to draw humans toward the Kingdom, not by force but through the Gospel.

sens: One who fishes, who captures fish
Figuratively, one who seeks to capture or catch something
H1771.detail:
1. It primarily refers to a person who practices the profession of fishing, capturing fish in the water with nets or hooks. In Isaiah 19:8, the "fishermen" who cast hooks into the river and spread nets over the waters are professionals or workers in river fishing, affected by the announced calamity. It is a well-known and recognizable profession in ancient Egypt.
2. The Bible also uses this word figuratively for one who captures people themselves: in Jeremiah 16:16, the Lord sends "fishermen" to "fish" for the Israelites in judgment, meaning to catch them and take them away from their lands, just as one captures fish in a net. The image of the net transitions from nature to history: one pursues, encircles, removes, with the same effectiveness as a hunter or fisherman using their tools to master their prey.
H1771.origine: The word comes from the root "dag," which means "fish." A "fisherman" (dayag) is literally "one who deals with fish." This root is very ancient and common in Hebrew for all words related to fishing and fish. The same base word appears in other Semitic languages with the same meaning.
H1771.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Isaiah 19:8, in the context of judgment on Egypt and the drying up of the Nile, the fishermen of the river are mentioned as suffering from the plague: it is a people who live by fishing and find themselves ruined. In Jeremiah 16:16, the word is used metaphorically: God sends "fishermen" and "hunters" to capture the Israelites and exile them, transforming an ordinary profession into an image of divine judgment. In both cases, the fisherman is a man who possesses the means and technique to capture what he aims for.
H1771.portee: This image of the fisherman invites the reader to reflect on the power and scope of divine judgment: God has the means and determination of a professional to accomplish His purposes. It also shows that no one can escape this judgment, just as a fish cannot flee the net laid out. For the believer, it is a call to take seriously the word of the Lord.

sens: Large carnivorous bird with gray or brown plumage that feeds on carrion
Biblical image of the power of destruction and desolation
H1772.detail:
1. The vulture is a large bird of prey with a powerful beak and formidable claws, which hunts or feeds on dead animals. In Deuteronomy 14:13, it appears in the list of unclean birds that the Israelites must not eat, alongside other birds of prey. It is a wild, free animal that obeys only its survival instincts.
2. In biblical texts, the vulture embodies desolation and divine judgment. In Isaiah 34:15, at the heart of a vision of total ruin of the land of Edom, vultures gather to lay and cover their eggs in the ruins — an apocalyptic image where nature reclaims the devastated lands, a living testimony of abandonment and God's judgment.
H1772.origine: The Hebrew word dayyah comes from a root evoking rapid movement or hunting. It is a generic term for birds of prey; the translation as "vulture" follows the tradition of the Segond. The biblical context shows that it refers to a large feared raptor, not a small bird.
H1772.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Deuteronomy 14:13, it is listed among the unclean birds, which shows that the Israelites were well acquainted with this animal and considered it ritually impure, thus unfit for consumption — a simple legal and practical mention. In Isaiah 34:15, its use is highly symbolic: vultures nest in the ruins of conquered Edom, illustrating the irreversibility of divine judgment and the transformation of the land into a desert inhabited only by beasts. Between these two uses, the tone shifts from legal to prophetic.
H1772.portee: The vulture reminds us that divine judgment on sin is real and complete: it is not an abstract threat, but a reality embodied in the fall of empires and the desolation of rebellious lands. For the believer, this image invites respect for God's warnings and not to confuse His patience with indifference.

sens: Colored liquid used for writing
Black mark left by writing
What makes the word durable and transmissible
H1773.detail: 1. Ink is the black liquid applied to papyrus or parchment to trace letters. In Jeremiah 36:18, Baruch recounts how he wrote the prophet's words "with ink" — it is the physical act of writing that fixes the dictated words onto the medium. 2. Ink also evokes a lasting trace, the permanent nature of what is written. Unlike spoken words that dissipate, ink engraves on the medium and persists. 3. In the prophetic context, ink symbolizes faithful transmission: what Baruch writes in ink becomes a lasting testimony of God's words, protected from forgetfulness and distortion.
H1773.origine: The Hebrew word דְּיוֹ (deyo) simply refers to the substance with which one writes. Its etymology is uncertain, but it belongs to the realm of writing — a fundamental domain in biblical culture where fixing God's words in writing is a sacred act. The same word appears in Egyptian and Aramaic papyri, attesting to the importance of writing in the ancient world.
H1773.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible: in Jeremiah 36:18. It is found in a decisive scene where the prophet Jeremiah orders Baruch to write the scroll containing all his words. This act of writing in ink takes on a prophetic dimension: the written words will survive the destruction of Jerusalem and testify to God's warning. Ink here is the concrete means by which the prophetic word becomes indestructible.
H1773.portee: For the Christian reading this account, ink reminds us that God makes His word endure. The words written in ink by Baruch cannot be annihilated — they will reach us intact centuries later. It is a meditation on God's faithfulness to preserve His message for all time.

sens: Location situated on the border of Moab
H1774.detail: 1. Di-Zahab is a place mentioned only once in the Bible, as a geographical landmark during Moses' farewell speech to the Israelites (Deuteronomy 1:1). The name literally means "enough gold" in Hebrew, but it refers to a concrete site, probably a region or camping area in the Transjordan desert, on the border of Moab, east of the Jordan.
H1774.origine: The Hebrew name דִּי זָהָב (di zahav) consists of two words: דִּי (di), meaning "enough" or "sufficient," and זָהָב (zahav), meaning "gold." This combination suggests a place abundant in gold, or at least a location thus named by the ancient Israelites. The meaning of the name may reflect an ancient tradition or a notable characteristic of the site.
H1774.emploi: Di-Zahab appears only once in the entire Bible, in Deuteronomy 1:1, where Moses lists the locations in the Transjordan desert as landmarks of the territory traversed during the forty years of wandering. The name appears in a list of localities (Suph, Paran, Tophel, Laban, Hazeroth) that geographically situate Moses' speech. Although mentioned only once, this place attested to a reality known to the Israelites and their descendants.

sens: City of Moab, in Transjordan
H1775.detail: 1. Dimon is a city located in Moab, a region east of the Jordan. It appears in the context of a prophetic oracle announcing divine judgment on Moab (Isaiah 15:9). The name evokes either a riverbed or silence — two images that may suggest future desolation.
H1775.origine: The name Dimon is a spelling variant of Dibon (another name for the same city). The word may derive from a root meaning "riverbed" or "silence," images of desert and devastation. This city was an important place in Moab, hence its appearance in prophetic texts announcing the fate of this region.
H1775.emploi: Dimon appears only once in the Bible, in Isaiah 15:9, in an oracle of the prophet against Moab. This passage uses the name of the city to symbolize the judgment that will fall upon the entire country: "The waters of Dimon are full of blood." The use of the geographical proper name gives the prophecy a concrete and historical significance — it is not an abstract threat, but a calamity that will reach this territory and its inhabitants.

sens: City in southern Judah
H1776.detail: Dimona is a small city located in the Negev region, in the southern part of the territory of Judah. It appears in the list of cities assigned to the tribe of Judah during the division of the promised land.
H1776.origine: The Hebrew name Dimona (דִּימוֹנָה) likely means "dried-up bed" or "silence," evoking an arid landscape characteristic of southern Palestine. The city derives its name from the desert geography of the region.
H1776.emploi: Dimona is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Joshua 15:22, in the midst of a enumeration of cities assigned to Judah during the conquest of Canaan. It is listed among the small localities of the Negev, alongside Kina and Adada, indicating its minor role in biblical administrative geography.

sens: To exercise the function of a judge, to render a judicial decision
To defend someone's cause, to plead for them
To execute judgment, to punish or vindicate
To govern, to administer a people
To contest, to enter into conflict with someone
H1777.detail:
1. To judge is primarily to sit as a judge and render a decision on a dispute (Psalms 7:9: "The Lord judges the peoples"). It is to evaluate a situation and decide according to law and justice.
2. To defend someone is to plead their cause, to take their side, like a lawyer before the court (Proverbs 31:9: "Open your mouth, judge righteously, and plead the cause of the poor"). The judge does not merely condemn; he can also protect the innocent.
3. To execute judgment is to implement the sentence, to punish the guilty or to vindicate and protect the just (Deuteronomy 32:36: "The Lord will judge His people"). This judgment can be severe as discipline, or gentle as deliverance.
4. To govern is to judge as a leader who administers a people with authority and justice (Psalms 72:2: "He will judge your people with righteousness"). Just governance is a permanent judgment.
5. To contest is to enter into conflict or quarrel with someone, to have a dispute (Genesis 30:6: Rachel says, "God has judged me" in relation to her rival Leah). This is a rarer sense and closer to conflict than to official decision.
H1777.origine: The verb din comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of cutting, of untangling what opposes. It is related to words of the same family that denote judgment and dispute. The Aramaic equivalent din (דִּין) carries the same meaning. In the Greek Bible of the Old Testament, this verb is often translated by forms of krinô (κρίνω), which also means to judge and to decide.
H1777.emploi: This verb appears 24 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the Psalms, historical books, and prophets. It primarily denotes the action of the Lord judging His people (Deuteronomy 32:36, Psalms 96:10), often to protect or correct them according to His justice. Human kings and judges must also judge fairly (Proverbs 31:9, Jeremiah 21:12). In Genesis 6:3, the verb has the weaker sense of "to remain" (my spirit will not remain), showing that the word can also mean to dwell or persist. The usage shifts between formal judicial judgment, defense of the oppressed, and just governance.
H1777.portee: This word reminds believers that God is the true judge, just and impartial, and that true justice must defend the weak and the oppressed, never favor the powerful. For a leader or magistrate, judging according to the law obliges one to seek equity and to protect those who cannot defend themselves. It is an invitation to abandon false accusations and to place trust in the One who sees all and judges wisely.

sens: Judgment according to the law, rendered by a competent authority
Application of law and legality
Equity and impartiality in human affairs
H1778.detail:
1. The word "justice" primarily refers to the judgment itself, the act of resolving a dispute or an accusation according to the laws in force. In Ezra 7:25, the king asks Ezra to appoint judges capable of "rendering justice" to the people, meaning to pronounce just judgments based on God's Law.
2. By extension, it is the correct application of the law: rendering justice means establishing order and legality, distinguishing the guilty from the innocent, the just from the unjust. It is a function of authority.
3. The term also evokes equity, moral uprightness: authentic justice requires that the one who judges be impartial and truly know the laws they must apply.
H1778.origine: The Aramaic word "din" comes from an ancient Semitic root meaning "to judge" or "to decide." It is used in biblical Aramaic to refer both to the act of judging and the judgment rendered. This word appears rarely in the Old Testament, particularly in passages where Aramaic is used (such as the book of Ezra), reflecting the administrative and judicial use of this language.
H1778.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible in Ezra 7:25, in a very clear official and legal context: the Persian king Artaxerxes orders Ezra to appoint judges who will render justice according to God's Law to the people beyond the river. The usage emphasizes that justice is a serious institution, entrusted to competent individuals who know divine laws. It is an act of authority and moral responsibility.
H1778.portee: This word reminds the believer of the importance of justice in community life: God desires that His people be governed according to true justice, based on His Law, not on arbitrariness or corruption. It is a call to seek equity and uprightness in all circumstances, especially for those who exercise authority.

sens: Decision of a judge that resolves a dispute or condemns a guilty party
Dispute, trial, matter brought before justice
Cause or right of someone in a litigation
The exercise of authority and governance in equity
Condemnation, punishment
H1779.detail:
1. Judgment is the sentence pronounced by a judge or a competent authority: it is the result of examining a case. Psalms 76:9 speaks of the "sentence" proclaimed from the heavens, showing that God Himself judges and condemns.

2. The dispute or trial itself is also called "judgment": it is the contentious matter brought to justice. Deuteronomy 17:8 refers to a "cause" too difficult to resolve, meaning a complex litigation that requires a legal decision.

3. The right of a person in a trial — their cause, their interest — bears this name. Proverbs 29:7 states that "the righteous knows the cause of the poor": he understands and defends their legitimate right against oppression.

4. To govern justly also means to exercise equitable judgment: it is to maintain order through right decisions. Proverbs 20:8 describes the king on his throne of justice who "dispels all evil with his gaze".

5. The punishment that results from judgment is conflated with the judgment itself. Job 19:29 reminds that "the sword" brings terrible punishments, marks of divine judgment on evil.
H1779.origine: The Hebrew word *din* primarily denotes the action of judging and rendering justice. It comes from a root that expresses the idea of deciding with authority. In the Old Testament, this term is very ancient and fundamental: it also appears in Aramaic with the same meaning. The word evokes the image of the judge who examines both parties and pronounces a word that resolves the dispute.
H1779.emploi: This word appears 17 times in the Old Testament, especially in the wisdom literature (Proverbs, Job, Psalms) and in the prophetic writings. It is used in two contexts: first legal and procedural (a cause, a trial to resolve), then theological and royal (God's judgment, the exercise of governance). Translations vary according to the context: "cause" or "right" when speaking of the litigation itself, "judgment" when emphasizing the decision, "justice" when the focus is on equity. The passages show that the justice of the poor and the equity of the king are forms of divine judgment.
H1779.portee: This word reminds every Christian that justice is not an abstraction: it is realized in the defense of the weak and in the decisions that establish equity. It belongs first to God, who judges with authority, but it is also the responsibility of the ruler and the righteous who must defend the oppressed. Understanding biblical "judgment" calls for reconciling the fear of divine judgment with the practical love of one's neighbor in justice.

sens: decision or sentence of a court
justice, equity
the right, what is just
coming of divine judgment
H1780.detail:
1. In the strict sense, it is the sentence pronounced by a judge or authority: one who transgresses the law will be "condemned" to death, exile, a fine, or imprisonment (Ezra 7:26). It is the verdict that is executed.
2. The word also denotes justice itself, the equity that characterizes the one who judges: the ways of the Most High are "just," because He acts with uprightness (Daniel 4:37).
3. It signifies the right, what belongs to someone justly: the Ancient of Days came to give "right" to the saints, meaning to restore what rightfully belongs to them (Daniel 7:22).
4. By extension, it is the coming of judgment itself, the act of judging: "the judgment of the Most High will come" upon the empires of the world (Daniel 7:26).
H1780.origine: This Aramaic word derives from the same root as the Hebrew din (judgment). It comes from a fundamental legal image: that of the judge who examines, weighs, and decides between two parties. In both Hebrew and Aramaic, this root emphasizes the act of rendering justice, of resolving the dispute.
H1780.emploi: The word appears five times in the Aramaic portions of the Bible (Ezra and Daniel). It is used primarily in Daniel 7, the great passage of the four beasts and eschatological judgment. Ezra 7 uses it regarding the judicial power of the king. In all cases, it refers to true judgment, whether human and legal, or divine and final. Its meaning varies slightly: the executed sentence, the justice of the judge, the right of the oppressed restored, or the awaited judgment.
H1780.portee: This word reminds that God judges with equity and retribution. For the believer, it assures that injustices do not go unpunished and that the rights of the saints will be restored. It is a comfort in the face of unjust earthly powers: true judgment comes from God alone.

sens: one who renders justice, who decides between two parties
one who defends the cause of an oppressed or unprotected person
H1781.detail: 1. The judge is primarily one who exercises judicial authority: he listens to both parties in conflict and renders a judgment that resolves their dispute (1 Samuel 24:16: David says that the Lord "will judge" between him and Saul). 2. This word also refers to one who defends a weak or abandoned person: it is a protector who guarantees their rights. It is in this sense that God is called the "defender" of widows and orphans, meaning one who watches over their justice against those who might oppress them (Psalms 68:6).
H1781.origine: This Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to judge" or "to decide." Its Aramaic equivalent exists in the Aramaic portions of the Bible. The concept of a judge dates back to the judicial institutions of Israel, where judges had a dual function: to apply the law and to protect the weak whom no one defended.
H1781.emploi: This word appears twice in the Old Testament. In 1 Samuel 24:16, it refers to the Lord in His role as the supreme judge who will decide the dispute between David and Saul. In Psalms 68:6, it describes God as the defender of orphans and widows, emphasizing not the judicial sentence but the active protection of those who are vulnerable. Both uses highlight that the true judge does not pronounce cold judgments: he supports the one who is in the right.
H1781.portee: This word invites the reader to recognize that God is not a distant and impartial judge, but an active defender of the oppressed and the weak. For the believer in danger or distress, this means that God takes their cause to heart and will act to render them justice. It also urges us to imitate this mercy: we too are called to defend those who cannot defend themselves.

sens: Officer responsible for administering justice
Judge who applies and teaches the law
H1782.detail: 1. A magistrate is a public officer established to administer justice and resolve disputes among the inhabitants. It is someone to whom judicial authority is entrusted in a region or province. In Ezra 7:25, the king of Persia charges Ezra with establishing magistrates to judge all the peoples beyond the river according to the laws of God. 2. The magistrate does not only judge: he also teaches the law to those who do not know it. His role is to make known and enforce the rules, particularly the religious laws of God's people. He is a judicial leader and an instructor.
H1782.origine: This Aramaic word "dayyan" comes from a root that means "to judge" (din). It is the same word as in Hebrew (H1781), where it designates the judge. It is rooted in the idea of rendering a judgment, of resolving a dispute. In the Greek Old Testament, this word translates Hebrew terms related to justice and governance.
H1782.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Ezra 7:25, an Aramaic text. It is King Artaxerxes who orders Ezra to establish magistrates to judge. The context is that of the restoration of Jerusalem after the exile: these magistrates must apply God's laws to all the peoples of the region beyond the river, including non-Jews. The term designates an official, administrative, and religious position at the same time.
H1782.portee: This passage shows that justice comes from God and must be rendered according to His law, even by human authorities foreign to God's people. It is a reminder that magistrates and judges are responsible not only for maintaining order but also for teaching and living out divine justice.

sens: daughter of Jacob and Leah
woman of the patriarchal era whose story reveals family violence and vengeance
H1783.detail: Dina is the daughter that Leah bore to Jacob (Genesis 30:21), the only daughter mentioned among Jacob's children. Her story, recounted in chapter 34 of Genesis, is marked by a tragic event: while going out to see the daughters of the land, she is seduced (or raped) by Shechem, the son of the king of the Hivites (Genesis 34:1-3). This dishonorable act triggers terrible vengeance: her brothers Simeon and Levi, under the pretext of negotiating for a marriage, kill all the males of the city of Shechem (Genesis 34:25-26). Her name means "judgment" in Hebrew, which resonates significantly with the divine judgment that her misadventure seems to attract upon Jacob's family.
H1783.origine: The name Dina (דִּינָה) comes from the Hebrew root דִּין (din), which means "to judge" or "judgment." This is the only place in the Hebrew Bible where this feminine name appears; it symbolizes the idea of divine justice. The root evokes the Lord's intervention in the face of injustice, making the account of her violation and the ensuing vengeance particularly poignant.
H1783.emploi: Dina is mentioned eight times in the Bible, all in Genesis. She first appears simply at her birth (Genesis 30:21), then at the center of the drama in chapter 34, where she becomes the focus of a major family crisis. The story reveals how an act of violence against a young woman triggers bloody vengeance: her brothers Simeon and Levi kill the men of Shechem, an act that Jacob himself will later disapprove (Genesis 49:5-7). Dina herself disappears from the narrative after this drama; it is unknown whether she survived or what fate befell her. Her name reappears one last time in Genesis 46:15, in the list of Jacob's children who go down to Egypt.
H1783.portee: The story of Dina challenges the reader regarding the vulnerability of women in ancient societies, the price of family honor, and the cycles of violence that sin provokes. It also shows how Jacob and his family, despite divine election, remain prisoners of human passions and carnal vengeance. For the believer, this account invites reflection on the grace of God that persists despite the failings of His elect.

sens: People or region of the Persian empire, contemporary with the reconstruction of the temple in Jerusalem
H1784.detail: 1. Din designates a people or region of the Persian empire whose representatives are mentioned as adversaries of the reconstruction of the Jewish temple during the time of Ezra. These "Din" appear alongside other peoples (Babylonians, Susans, Elamites…) in a letter written to the Persian king to thwart the work in Jerusalem. The precise location of Din is unknown, but it was clearly a group of peoples from the Persian empire of the 5th century B.C.
H1784.origine: The Aramaic word דִּינָיֵא (dinaïa) appears only once in the Bible. Its exact etymology remains debated; it could be related to a term designating an ethnic or geographical group of the Achaemenid empire. The word appears only in the Aramaic text of Ezra, where it is transcribed as is.
H1784.emploi: This people appears only once in Ezra 4:9, in a list of peoples and regions that send a delegation to oppose the reconstruction of the temple. These delegates write together a letter to the king in an attempt to stop the work. This is the only information the Bible provides about the Din: we know neither their precise location nor their history, other than that they were part of the Persian empire and were concerned about the growing power of the Jews returned from exile.

sens: Fortified structure built around a city to keep it besieged
Defensive work constructed or reinforced by the besiegers
H1785.detail:
1. The entrenchment is a fortification or barrier built by besieging soldiers around a city to enclose it and prevent any exit or resupply. It is a siege work, often associated with ramps and battering rams that allow for attacking the city walls (see Ezekiel 4:2 where it is raised against Jerusalem). The word evokes the image of trenches or walls that are "dug" or "raised" to encircle the enemy.
2. By extension, the entrenchment can also refer to any fortified defensive or encircling structure built during a military siege. In Ezekiel 26:8, the entrenchment is formed by the king of Tyre against a city, showing that this term applies to military engineering works in general during a siege.
H1785.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to pierce" or "to dig," hence the idea of a structure that is "dug" or "embedded" in the ground. This image of dug or raised works for the siege is at the heart of the word. It appears exclusively in contexts of military siege, notably in the prophets describing the sieges of Jerusalem and Tyre by the Babylonians.
H1785.emploi: The word appears 6 times in the Hebrew Bible, only in the context of military siege. It is concentrated in the prophetic books: Jeremiah (1 time) and Ezekiel (4 times), as well as in 2 Kings (1 time). The two occurrences in 2 Kings 25:1 and Jeremiah 52:4 describe the same historical event — the siege of Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar — and mention the entrenchment as a fortification that the Babylonian army "raises all around." In the passages from Ezekiel, the entrenchment systematically appears alongside other elements of the siege (ramps, battering rams, camps), forming a technical vocabulary of ancient siege. The word remains technical and has no figurative meaning: it always describes material realities of war.
H1785.portee: This word reminds the reader of the overwhelming power of the besieging armies, and the inevitability of God's judgment on rebellious cities. The prophets use it to concretely show how Jerusalem and the enemy nations will be reduced by inexorable means of war. It is a lesson on the reality of sin and its visible and destructive consequences.

sens: the action of separating the wheat grains from the chaff
figuratively, a period of intense work or activity
H1786.detail:
1. The threshing of wheat is the operation that consists of separating the wheat grains from the chaff and straw after the harvest. In Leviticus 26:5, the text evokes a time of blessing so abundant that "you will hardly have threshed the wheat before you begin the harvest" — the threshing takes so little time that the harvesters begin their work already, so rich is the harvest.
2. By extension, the word designates work or activity, often intense or pressing. In the same verse, the abundance of successive harvests creates a continuity of labor, so that the threshing of wheat directly follows the harvest without interruption.
H1786.origine: The Hebrew word דַּיִשׁ (dayish) comes from a root expressing the idea of beating, striking, or grinding. This root evokes the concrete image of a flail or trampling that separates the grain from its chaff. The word is formed to specifically designate the process of threshing, that is, the stage of agricultural work where the freshly harvested grain is processed to be usable.
H1786.emploi: This word appears only once in Leviticus 26:5 in the provided French New Testament. It is found in a passage of divine blessing: God promises Israel a harvest so abundant that the threshing of wheat will overlap with the harvest — an image of prosperity and security. The context is that of a people obeying the Lord's laws, to whom He grants an overflowing material blessing where even the most demanding work follows without a break.
H1786.portee: This passage reminds the Christian reader that divine blessing far exceeds what is necessary: it creates an abundance. The promise invites trust in God rather than fear of lack, and it shows that obedience to His commandments brings not only the satisfaction of need but also security and prosperity. It is a call to see God's provision as real and abundant.

sens: Chief Horite of the land of Edom during the time of the Patriarchs
Son of Seir
H1787G.detail:
1. Dishon is a name of individuals who lived during the time of the Patriarchs. The text designates him as one of the chiefs of the Horites, a people established in the land of Edom (Genesis 36:21, 30). He appears in the list of descendants of Seir and is presented with the title of chief, indicating a position of authority or responsibility among the Horites.
2. According to the genealogy in Genesis 36, Dishon was a son of Seir and thus a brother of several other Horite chiefs: Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, Anah, Ezer, and Dishan. The repeated mention of his name both in Genesis 36:21 and verse 30 shows his importance in this family and clan structure of the peoples of Edom.
H1787G.origine: The name Dishon literally means "one who winnows" or "thresher" in English — an image drawn from the action of separating grain from chaff. This name possibly reflects an activity or characteristic of an ancestor. The mentioned genealogy also attests to a variant form of the name, Dishan (דִּישָׁן), which sometimes designates the same character or a person from the same genealogical cycle.
H1787G.emploi: Dishon appears three times in the Bible, always in genealogical lists: twice in Genesis 36 (verses 21 and 30) and once in 1 Chronicles 1:38. These three occurrences systematically present him as chief of the Horites, descendants of Seir who inhabited the territory of Edom before the dominance of the Edomites. His name returns in a slightly different form (Dishan), reflecting the common spelling variants in biblical genealogies. These genealogical lists served to document the history of peoples and kingdoms in the Levant region.

sens: man living in the time of the patriarchs, member of the family of Edom
H1787I.detail: Dischan is a descendant of Seir the Horite, appearing in the genealogy of ancient peoples of the Middle East. His name appears only once in the Bible in 1 Chronicles 1:42, where he is mentioned as the father of Uz and Aran, classifying him among the ancestors of the Edomite peoples who inhabited the region of Mount Seir.
H1787I.origine: The name Dischan literally means "one who winnows" or "one who separates grain," evoking the ancient image of grain work. It is a typical Semitic name found in Edomite genealogies. The name also appears in the form Dishon (H1787), a spelling variant of the same character.
H1787I.emploi: Dischan is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 1:42, in the context of a genealogy listing the descendants of Seir. There is no anecdote or narrative dedicated to him: his name simply appears in the list of ancestors of ancient peoples. This brief mention serves to document the origins of the peoples who lived before Israel.

sens: wild animal of the ungulate family, considered clean according to the Law
mountain antelope or gazelle with poorly defined characteristics
H1788.detail:
1. The deer is a wild hoofed animal, permissible to eat according to the Law of Moses: it is listed among the animals that an Israelite may eat (Deuteronomy 14:5). It is considered a clean animal, unlike those that do not chew the cud or do not have split hooves.
2. The exact identification of this animal remains uncertain: it is probably an antelope or a gazelle living in the mountains of Canaan, perhaps similar to the ibex, but its precise morphology eludes us. The Hebrew term designates an animal known to the Israelites in their geographical context, even if we can no longer determine it with certainty.
H1788.origine: The Hebrew word dîshôn comes from a root whose basic meaning remains obscure. Its exact etymology is debated; it may be related to names of wild animals in the Levant region. It appears in biblical nomenclatures of creatures, without appearing in other contexts of the preserved Hebrew text.
H1788.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible: in Deuteronomy 14:5, at the heart of a legislative enumeration. Moses lists the hoofed land animals that the Israelites are allowed to consume. The deer is mentioned alongside the gazelle, the ibex, and the giraffe. Its unique mention shows that it is a well-known beast among the ancient inhabitants of the Levant, integrated into the permitted diet, but this beast has likely disappeared or its identification has been lost.
H1788.portee: This mention of deer in the Law reminds us that God has established clear distinctions between what is suitable and what is not for His people, even in seemingly everyday matters like food. The text invites the reader to recognize that divine will extends to all areas of life, and that these boundaries have spiritual significance: eating clean animals symbolizes separation from impurity.

sens: Horite chief, son of Seir
Man of the patriarchal era
H1789G.detail: 1. Dischan is a Horite chief mentioned in the genealogy of Edom: he is one of the seven sons of Seir, alongside Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, Anah, Dishon, and Ezer (Genesis 36:21). His name literally means "thresher" or "one who beats grain," evoking a working man. 2. He is presented as a character living in the time of the Patriarchs: he himself has two sons, Uz and Aran (Genesis 36:28), and is recognized as a chief with an official title among the Horites who inhabited the land of Edom before the Edomites arrived (Genesis 36:30; 1 Chronicles 1:38).
H1789G.origine: The name "Dischan" (in Hebrew דִּישָׁן) literally means "thresher" or "one who beats," from the root evoking the threshing of grain. This term designates an Edomite ancestor whose name also appears in the variant "Dishon" in the same genealogical texts, both forms referring to the same person from the patriarchal era.
H1789G.emploi: Dischan is mentioned four times in Scripture, only in the genealogies of Edom: twice in Genesis 36 (verses 21 and 28), once in Genesis 36:30 among the "chiefs of the Horites," and once in 1 Chronicles 1:38 in the list of the sons of Seir. He represents one of the seven leading Horite families that occupied the land of Edom before the descendants of Esau settled there. These genealogical texts emphasize his role as a father and recognized chief.

sens: Son of Seir, Horite ancestor of the patriarchal era
H1789H.detail: Dishon is a character mentioned in the genealogy of the Horites, these ancient inhabitants of the region of Edom. He is the son of Seir and the brother of Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, Anah, Ezer, and Timna. He himself has four sons: Hemdan, Eschban, Jithran, and Karen (Genesis 36:26). His name, which means "one who winnows" or "winnower" (evoking the action of separating grain from chaff), reflects an ordinary human activity, but Dishon belongs to a lineage of ancestors whose memory has been preserved in Scripture to establish the kinship ties of the peoples who inhabited the territory that the Israelites were to occupy.
H1789H.origine: The name Dishon (or Dishon in Hebrew דִּישֹׁן) literally means "winnower" or "one who winnows," derived from a root expressing the action of winnowing grain. This personal name reflects a common activity in ancient agricultural life. Dishon is a spelling variant of the same name (both forms דִּישָׁן and דִּישֹׁן coexist in the Hebrew text). His appearance in the genealogy of the Horites is part of the picture of the peoples who populated Canaan before the arrival of Israel.
H1789H.emploi: Dishon appears only once in the Bible, in Genesis 36:26, in the list of the sons of Seir, the founder of the Horite nation. This genealogy is found in the passage dedicated to the descendants of Seir and their chiefs, which establishes a picture of the peoples settled in the region of Edom before the arrival of the descendants of Esau. His inclusion in this genealogical record shows that the Bible is interested in these earlier peoples and their lineages, even if they play no active role in the history of salvation.

sens: One who is physically or morally crushed by a superior force
One who suffers injustice and exploitation
One who is humiliated and defenseless
H1790.detail:
1. The word first evokes the image of someone crushed, rendered powerless by the weight of a force. It is the state of one who cannot rise: in Psalms 9:10, the Lord becomes "a refuge for the oppressed," one who needs protection because he is powerless.
2. It designates one who suffers injustice and oppression, a victim of one who abuses his power. In Proverbs 26:28, "a false tongue crushes" the one who suffers it, making him a victim of lies and betrayal.
3. It is the state of total weakness, where the person can neither defend himself nor obtain justice on his own. In Psalms 10:18, the oppressed can only rely on God for "the man drawn from the earth" (the oppressor) to cease doing harm.
H1790.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of being crushed, flattened, rendered weak. It is related to the physical image of something heavy pressing down and reducing. The term paints a state of humiliation and lack of strength, whether caused by external oppression or by circumstances.
H1790.emploi: This word appears 4 times in the Bible, always to describe one who suffers from injustice or oppression. The Psalms use it to speak of one who seeks refuge in God (Psalms 9:10; 10:18; 74:21), a recurring theme in the prayers of the persecuted. In Proverbs 26:28, it describes one who is a victim of lies. The oppressed is systematically presented as defenseless, needing God's intervention or justice to be rescued.
H1790.portee: This word reminds the reader that God hears the cry of those crushed by injustice and exploitation. It invites the believer to recognize that God stands with the weak and defenseless, and to refuse to oppress others. It is also a word of comfort for those who suffer: they are not alone, and their weakness is not a shame in the eyes of God.

sens: This object, person, or situation being referred to
This state of affairs, this circumstance that results
H1791.detail:
1. The word simply designates what is near or what is being talked about: "this city" (Ezra 4:13), "this house of the great God" (Ezra 5:8). It is the gesture of showing or pointing to what is present or in mind, as when one says "this one".
2. Sometimes it reinforces the link between a cause and its consequences, as in Ezra 5:16: "by this very thing" or "therefore," to indicate that what precedes leads to what follows.
H1791.origine: It is the Aramaic dekh, which corresponds to the Hebrew zeh ("this one," "this"). In the books of Ezra and Daniel, partially written in Aramaic, this word replaces the ordinary Hebrew form. It comes from a root that expresses the idea of showing or pointing out.
H1791.emploi: The word appears eleven times, only in the book of Ezra, in the Aramaic passages (chapters 4 to 6). It is used to designate the city of Jerusalem and its house (the Temple) during the correspondence between the Persian authorities and the Jews: "this city has risen against the kings" (Ezra 4:19), "this house of God" (Ezra 5:8). The context is that of the reconstruction of the Temple after the exile.
H1791.portee: This word shows us how the Aramaic texts of the Bible affirm the identity and importance of Jerusalem and the Temple, even amid negotiations with foreign powers. It emphasizes the concrete reality of what is being built or questioned.

sens: To break or reduce something into pieces by force
To tread upon, to walk on something
To oppress someone, to mistreat them
To be morally broken, to have a contrite and humbled heart
H1792.detail:
1. To crush primarily means to physically reduce something into pieces or flatten it by weight or force. This is the concrete image of the word: a worm that is crushed (Job 4:19), something that is trampled underfoot (Psalms 143:3).
2. In the sense of treading, the verb describes the action of walking on something or someone with contempt and violence, holding it underfoot, reducing it to nothing by overwhelming force.
3. To crush also takes on a moral and social meaning: to oppress someone, to mistreat them, to abuse them. An oppressor crushes the unfortunate and the poor who cannot defend themselves (Psalms 72:4; Isaiah 3:15).
4. Figuratively, to be crushed means to be broken inside, to have a contrite heart — that is, to be profoundly humble before God, recognizing one's nothingness. God dwells with the contrite and humbled man (Isaiah 57:15), and it is this state of heart that pleases God.
H1792.origine: The Hebrew verb dâkâ (דָּכָא) comes from a root that evokes the physical image of grinding, flattening, crushing — as one crushes grain or an insect. The word belongs to a family of Hebrew terms expressing destruction and humiliation. Its usage moves from the concrete (physically crushing) to the figurative (morally breaking), a natural movement in biblical Hebrew.
H1792.emploi: The verb dâkâ appears 18 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the wisdom books and the Psalms, as well as among the prophets. In the book of Job, it describes physical crushing (Job 4:19) and the act of mistreating someone with words (Job 19:2). The Psalms use it to describe the action of trampling a person underfoot (Psalms 143:3) or crushing the oppressor (Psalms 72:4). In Isaiah, the word takes on a profound theological dimension: in Isaiah 57:15, being contrite signifies the spiritual state of the humble believer who depends entirely on God. In Isaiah 53:5 and 53:10, it is the suffering servant of the Lord who is crushed — a prophecy about the humiliation and suffering of Christ for our salvation.
H1792.portee: This word teaches us that the physical and moral crushing of the weak is a serious sin before God, who defends the oppressed. But it also shows us that contrition — this breaking of the heart before God — is the spiritual attitude that God honors and with which He dwells. To be crushed by God is to lose all pretense of saving ourselves and to accept His forgiveness and grace.

sens: Spiritual state of one who is crushed by the weight of sin and remorse
Deep feeling of humiliation and repentance before God
Disposition of the heart that recognizes its guilt and unworthiness
H1793A.detail:
1. The man with a broken heart is literally crushed, flattened by the weight of his guilt. It is a state of deep moral distress where one feels annihilated before God. In Psalms 34:19, the one who has "a spirit of heaviness" has a heart thus broken: it is the condition of one who suffers, not only physically but spiritually.
2. This crushing of the heart engenders humility and contrition: one can no longer defend or justify oneself before the Lord. Isaiah 57:15 speaks of one who is "contrite and humbled," crushed by the awareness of his nothingness before the Most High.
3. It is precisely to one who is in this state that God shows Himself close and benevolent. Far from rejecting him, God dwells with the contrite man to "revive" his heart: the breaking of the heart becomes the place where God operates restoration and grace.
H1793A.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to crush," "to grind," or "to reduce to nothing." The image is that of something or someone flattened, crushed under a weight. This crushing is both physical (in suffering) and moral (in the awareness of sin). In biblical Hebrew, this state describes not only an external condition but the internal effect of divine judgment on the conscience.
H1793A.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. Both occurrences express the reaction of the soul before the evil committed and before God. In Psalms 34:19, the context is that of deliverance: the one who has a heart broken by suffering and remorse experiences that the Lord saves him. In Isaiah 57:15, the prophet announces that the Most High and Holy God, whose greatness is incomparable, paradoxically chooses to dwell with the one who is crushed by contrition. The breaking of the heart appears in these two passages as the prerequisite for receiving divine grace.
H1793A.portee: This word reveals a central truth of the Gospel: God does not reject one who is broken by remorse, but it is precisely there that He meets him. Far from being a state of despair, the broken heart becomes the place of restoration and divine tenderness. It is a word of hope for the sinner who surrenders to God without pretense.

sens: Fine powder that settles on the ground or objects
Fragile and light matter, without substance
Image of humility and human weakness before God
H1793B.detail: 1. Dust is the fine and light powder that covers the ground or accumulates on things: it is the most tenuous matter that disintegrates and flies away at the slightest breath. 2. By extension, it symbolizes what is fragile, perishable, easily destroyed: something without solidity or duration. 3. For humans, to be dust means to recognize one's own fragility and mortality before the eternal God. In Psalm 90:3, when God says "return to dust," He reminds that every man, despite his dignity, returns to that from which he came — the earth and humility.
H1793B.origine: The Hebrew word dak.ka is related to the idea of grinding, reducing to very fine particles. It evokes the most reduced matter, almost nothing: what remains after destruction or wear. It is a concrete word that paints the image of a substance without strength, freely carried away by the wind.
H1793B.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Psalm 90:3, one of the most profound psalms of meditation on the human condition and the passage of time. It is used by God Himself to say how men return to their source: not just any dust, but that which evokes the brevity of life and the nothingness of the creature before the Eternal. It is a rare and solemn word, reserved for this moment of truth.
H1793B.portee: This word invites the believer to a humble recognition of his finitude. In the face of the vanity of passing days, the mention of dust is not a message of despair, but of peace: it calls to seek God, the only one who remains, rather than to cling to things that crumble. For those who listen, it is an invitation to wisdom and trust.

sens: To crush or break into pieces by force
To bend, collapse under a weight or burden
To be broken morally or spiritually, to have a contrite heart
To destroy or completely annihilate
H1794.detail: 1. To break primarily means to crush something or reduce it to fragments: in Psalms 44:20, the psalmist says, "that you crush us in the den of jackals," an image of total destruction. 2. The word can also describe a physical collapse: in Psalms 10:10, the wicked "bends down, he stoops," his body collapsing under the weight of his wickedness. 3. Spiritually, to break denotes the contrition of the heart, the moral collapse before God: Psalms 38:9 says, "I am weak, utterly broken" — it is the inner rupture of the sinner who repents. 4. This verb also expresses complete destruction, the annihilation of a person or reality: Psalms 51:10, "the bones that you have broken will rejoice," evokes a total breaking followed by divine restoration.
H1794.origine: The Hebrew verb dakha comes from a root that paints the image of something collapsing, reducing to powder or debris. Its primary meaning is very concrete — to grind, to crush — but the Bible quickly uses it figuratively to describe the inner state of the heart broken by the conviction of sin. It is a popular word in the Psalms, particularly when the psalmist speaks of his own affliction or that which he suffers.
H1794.emploi: This verb appears five times in the provided passages, all in the book of Psalms. In Psalms 10:10 and 44:20, it describes a physical action of crushing, either of the wicked who bends down to drag his victims, or of God who crushes His people in punishment. In Psalms 38:9 and 51:10, 51:19, the meaning shifts inward: it is the heart, the spirit, the bones of the repentant sinner that are broken. Remarkably, this spiritual breaking becomes pleasing to God (Psalms 51:19) — it is the true sacrifice He accepts with favor, more than any burnt offering.
H1794.portee: The word break reminds the believer that true repentance is not an outward performance, but a breaking of the heart before God. Psalms 51:19 teaches that this contrition, this inner breaking of one who acknowledges his sin, is precisely what God desires and honors. It is a word of grace: spiritual breaking is not a definitive condemnation, but the path by which God restores the sincerely repentant sinner.

sens: state of that which has undergone strong compression, destruction by crushing
serious physical injury, bodily mutilation
H1795.detail:
1. The word literally denotes a crushing, a compression that destroys or deforms. In Deuteronomy 23:1, it describes crushed testicles, meaning mutilated or severely damaged — a physical injury that renders a man ritually impure according to the law of Moses.
2. More broadly, it evokes any form of grinding or destruction by compression: the image is of something crushed under a weight, reduced, annihilated.
H1795.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of pressing, crushing, grinding. This root paints the concrete image of a force that crushes, compresses to the point of destroying or mutilating. The form used here is a participle that describes the resulting state of this crushing.
H1795.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Deuteronomy 23:1, where it qualifies a genital mutilation that renders someone impure and excludes him from the assembly of worship. This passage is part of the purity laws of the people of Israel, which define who may participate in worship. The context shows that the law aimed to protect the physical integrity of the people and affirm the importance of bodily completeness for access to the sanctuary.
H1795.portee: This passage reminds us that, in the Old Testament, physical integrity was linked to the ability to serve God. For today's Christian, this invites meditation on the dignity of the human body according to the Bible, but also on how Jesus transformed the criteria of purity: it is the heart, not the physical state, that determines our access to God.

sens: The violent and repeated noise of waves crashing and breaking
The sound power of turbulent moving water
H1796.detail:
1. The word describes the crash made by rivers and waves when they collide forcefully — not just the movement of water, but the noise it produces as it crashes against the shores or breaks. In Psalms 93:3, the rivers "lift their roaring waves": the image is of the violent sound of raging water, a natural roar that rises to the heavens.
2. Figuratively, this "roaring" symbolizes power and majesty: these are not small streams that murmur, but rivers that thunder, witnesses to the indomitable force of creation.
H1796.origine: The Hebrew word dôkhi comes from a root expressing shock, crushing, the noise of something collapsing or breaking. The primary idea is that of destructive and noisy force — the echo of collision, of rupture. It is a rare word that captures the sound and violent aspect of the movement of waters.
H1796.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Psalms 93:3. It is used to magnify the greatness of the Lord: in the face of the psalmist contemplating the unleashed rivers, the hymn affirms that God is even more powerful than these unleashed forces. The context is a hymn of praise and trust in God despite earthly storms and fury.
H1796.portee: This word invites us to see in the grand spectacle of nature — the tumult of waters, the raw power — not a threat, but a testimony to the majesty of God. The roaring waves that would terrify a mortal become the chorus that sings the glory of the Creator, and teach us that our God reigns over all that makes the world tremble.

sens: that which is being spoken of by showing or designating it, putting it before the eyes
the particular object in question, in contrast with another
H1797.detail:
1. The word designates the object just mentioned or being indicated as present and remarkable. In Daniel 2:31, King Nebuchadnezzar looks at a gigantic statue and says: "this statue was immense" — he points with his hand to what he is actually seeing. It is the gesture of the finger pointing, of the gaze that fixes.
2. When several things are present, this word allows for specifying the one being spoken of now. In Daniel 7:20-21, among the ten horns of the beast, the prophet says: "this horn that had eyes" and then "I saw this horn making war against the saints" — he designates ONE particular horn, the one that is most remarkable and terrifying.
H1797.origine: It is the Aramaic equivalent of the Hebrew word "zeh" ("this, this one"), which belongs to the family of demonstratives — the words that show and designate. In both Hebrew and Aramaic, this word arises from the image of the pointed gesture of the finger towards the object. It comes from a very ancient root that etymologically means "to look" or "to see" — for to show is first to invite someone to look.
H1797.emploi: This word appears only 3 times, all in the book of Daniel, written in Aramaic. It is used in prophetic visions: when Daniel or King Nebuchadnezzar describe supernatural creatures or objects (the golden statue, the apocalyptic beasts), they use this demonstrative to focus attention. It is a narrative tool: the speaker says "this..." to mean "pay close attention to this one, this is the important one," distinguishing it from the others. Each time, it is to designate something terrifying or crucial for the meaning of the vision.
H1797.portee: This small word teaches us that the prophetic vision is not vague: it puts before the eyes of the seer precise realities that he can show, designate, describe in detail. When Daniel says "this horn," he conveys the immediacy and clarity of what he saw — it was not a blurry dream, but an encounter with the real, strange and terrible. For the reader, this invites taking seriously the details of prophecies: each demonstrative says "here is the fact," not an abstraction.

sens: Male sheep with spiral horns
Victim offered in sacrifice at the temple
H1798.detail:
1. The ram is a male sheep, recognizable by its large spiral horns. It is a domesticated animal raised for its wool and meat. In the three passages of Ezra, it is among the animals that the Jews returning from exile must provide or purchase: "two hundred rams" for the dedication of the temple (Ezra 6:17), or rams to be delivered daily to the priests for burnt offerings (Ezra 6:9).
2. The ram is an important sacrificial animal in the law of Moses. It was offered as a burnt offering (completely consumed) or as a sin offering. Its status as a male animal and its size made it a valuable offering, more prestigious than a lamb but less costly than a bull. In Ezra 7:17, rams are purchased "for the offerings and the libations," that is, to honor God through sacrifice.
H1798.origine: The Hebrew word דְּכַר (dekhar) literally means "male" — it comes from a root expressing strength and virility. It is found in other contexts to designate male animals (as opposed to females). This word emphasizes that it is an adult male animal that is offered, never a female, which meets the requirements of the sacrificial law: the victims must be without defect and of superior quality.
H1798.emploi: The word appears three times, only in Ezra 6 and 7, during the account of the return of the Jews after the Babylonian exile (circa 516 B.C.). These passages speak of the reconstruction and dedication of the second temple. The rams are listed with other animals — bulls and lambs — for the daily burnt offerings and dedication sacrifices. They reflect the prescriptions of the Law that the Jews were striving to uphold despite their limited resources upon returning from exile.
H1798.portee: The ram reminds us that the worship of God requires a sincere and costly offering from the people. Although the exiled Jews were impoverished, they restored the prescribed sacrifices by purchasing rams and other animals: this is an act of faithfulness and restoration of the covenant. For the Christian reader, these sacrifices foreshadow the ultimate sacrifice of Christ, the Lamb of God offered once for all.

sens: Written document recording important facts, orders, or decisions
Official register where memorable acts are noted
H1799A.detail:
1. The word refers to a written document — here a scroll — on which official information is recorded that one wants to preserve and transmit. In Ezra 6:2, the king of Persia orders that this record related to the temple be sought, showing that it is an administrative file kept in the royal archives. It is a text that can be read and reread to remember decisions made in the past.
2. More broadly, it is any register or memorial document where one inscribes what one does not want to forget — a kind of official record. The scroll found at Achmetha contains the decree of Cyrus regarding the reconstruction of the temple, an act so important that it is preserved in writing.
H1799A.origine: This Aramaic word (the official language of the Persian Empire) comes from the same Hebrew root זִכָּרוֹן *zikkaron* ("memorial"), which itself derives from the root זָכַר *zakhar* ("to remember"). Thus, a record is not just a document, but an object intended to revive memory, to prevent forgetfulness. The same family of words expresses the idea of "to recall" and "to keep in memory."
H1799A.emploi: This Aramaic word appears only once in the Bible, in Ezra 6:2. It is found in the context of the administrative affairs of the Persian Empire, when Darius orders a search of the royal archives. The record in question is the decree of Cyrus authorizing the reconstruction of the temple in Jerusalem — an act of supreme power that is recorded in writing so that no one may ignore it. This usage reflects the administrative practice of the time: important royal decrees were archived and accessible.
H1799A.portee: This passage shows how God works through the structures of human power: the king's decree is preserved in the archives, and it is by rereading it that the reconstruction of the temple is unlocked. For the believer, this illustrates that God's plans are not forgotten — they are inscribed, kept, and come to fruition in their time, even through the official actions of nations.

sens: Written document recording the facts, acts, or events of the past
Archive or official register kept to testify to what has occurred
What one remembers, preserved memory
H1799B.detail:
1. A record is a written document that registers and preserves important events or acts. In Ezra 4:15, the king of Persia requests that "the book of the records of your fathers" be consulted — an official register where the facts concerning Jerusalem and its past rebellion have been noted. It is an archival document intended to keep track of history.
2. By extension, it is an official register or list that one consults to verify facts and make decisions. The word evokes the image of a table, a register where everything is written down clearly so that it can be remembered and referred to long after.
3. Broadly speaking, record refers to the memory itself — the lasting trace that past events leave and that is voluntarily preserved.
H1799B.origine: This Aramaic word (used in Ezra 4:15, in the Aramaic portion of the book) is close to the Hebrew זִכָּרוֹן (zikaron, "memorial"), which comes from the root meaning "to remember." The family of the word revolves around the idea of keeping memory alive: a record is created so that what has been is not forgotten. This root also appears in Hebrew terms like מִזְכֶּרֶת (the memorial offering).
H1799B.emploi: This word appears only once in Ezra 4:15, in a letter that the adversaries of Judah send to the Persian king. They invoke the records, that is, the official archives of the court, to prove that Jerusalem has always been rebellious. It is an administrative argument: a written document, a register kept by the state, is presented as historical evidence. The context shows that the records are precise, consultable documents on which one can rely to justify a policy.
H1799B.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that God also keeps His own records: nothing escapes His memory, every act is recorded. It also invites vigilance: words and actions have consequences that are inscribed in history, and one must be aware of this.

sens: A living man during the time of the Patriarchs, son of Anah and grandson of Seir
H1787H.detail: 1. Dishon is a man from the family of Seir, who lived during the time of the Patriarchs. He is the son of Anah and the brother of Oholibamah (Genesis 36:25). His name means "one who winnows" or "one who separates the grain" in reference to the image of a winnower. He belongs to the lineage of the indigenous peoples of Canaan, the Horites, of whom Seir was the ancestor.
H1787H.origine: The name Dishon (Hebrew דִּישֹׁן) etymologically means "one who winnows" or "one who treads," evoking the action of threshing grain. This image may reflect an activity or a characteristic trait. The name appears in the genealogies of the Canaanite peoples in the Old Testament.
H1787H.emploi: Dishon is mentioned twice in the Bible: first in Genesis 36:25, where he is presented as one of the children of Anah, son of Seir and brother of Oholibamah. He reappears in 1 Chronicles 1:41, in the same repeated genealogy, where his own sons are listed: Hamran, Eshban, Jithran, and Keran. These two passages constitute the only place he occupies in the Scriptures, as a link in a genealogical chain that shows the indigenous peoples of Canaan before the conquest.
